Serious question for @CENTCOM...

How was the vessel attempting to run the blockade nearly 24 hours after it had turned away and transited m
events.description:
Serious question for @CENTCOM...

How was the vessel attempting to run the blockade nearly 24 hours after it had turned away and transited more than 250 miles in the opposite direction, in apparent compliance with directives?

Given the strike disabled the ship, it appears that the strike occurred off the coast of UAE.

The ship also spent ~5 hours loitering/drifting near the blockade line, before turning back toward the UAE.

HOLY CRAP! BUKELE’S EL SALVADOR ECONOMY SET TO OUTPERFORM NEIGHBORS FOR THE FIRST TIME IN 30 YEARS

El Salvador under President Nayib Bukele
events.description:
HOLY CRAP! BUKELE’S EL SALVADOR ECONOMY SET TO OUTPERFORM NEIGHBORS FOR THE FIRST TIME IN 30 YEARS

El Salvador under President Nayib Bukele is reportedly on track to outperform Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua economically for the first time in more than three decades. After cracking down on gangs and restoring security, Bukele says the country is attracting investment and transforming its economy, turning a nation once plagued by violent crime into a rising regional success story.

events.title: U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) said it disabled the Palau flagged bulk carrier M/V Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday, Nov. 26th
events.description:
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) said it disabled the Palau flagged bulk carrier M/V Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday, Nov. 26th, after the crew "attempted to run" the U.S. blockade following departure from Bandar Abbas, Iran.

AIS data from MarineTraffic shows the vessel was on course to exit the Gulf of Oman late Nov. 24th or early Nov. 25th when it turned sharply north and ran nearly parallel to the blockade line at 12.8 knots. At 0815 UTC it slowed to 0.6 knots, and at 1316 UTC it turned back into the Gulf of Oman at 5 to 6 knots.

At 2000 UTC on Nov. 25th (0000 local time on Nov. 26th), the vessel was about 70 nautical miles from the blockade line, heading into the Gulf of Oman at 4.9 knots. It continued toward the anchorage off Fujairah, United Arab Emirates (UAE), throughout Nov. 26th.

The data appears difficult to reconcile with CENTCOM's description of an attempt to run the blockade on Nov. 26th and appears to indicate that the strike was conducted as the vessel was transiting away from the blockade line. AIS is self reported and can be manipulated, however this vessel's track does not appear to show indicators of being spoofed.

events.title: U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) says U.S. forces disabled the Palau flagged bulk carrier Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman on Nov. 26 after
events.description:
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) says U.S. forces disabled the Palau flagged bulk carrier Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman on Nov. 26 after its crew tried to run the blockade of Iran despite multiple warnings. 

A U.S. military aircraft struck the ship's stern with precision munitions, disabling its propulsion. CENTCOM says the civilian crew was unharmed. 

The ship departed from Bandar Abbas, Iran. According to CENTCOM, it is the sixth vessel disabled since enforcement resumed in July. U.S. forces have also redirected 158 ships that complied.

events.title: A 38 year old Florida woman was arrested on Thanksgiving, after driving through the main gate of Hurlburt Field with a child in her vehicle
events.description:
A 38 year old Florida woman was arrested on Thanksgiving, after driving through the main gate of Hurlburt Field with a child in her vehicle and claiming to have explosives in her car, according to the Okaloosa County Sheriff's Office.

The sheriff's office says she parked on the installation and did not respond to Hurlburt Field Security Forces or deputies. Security Forces decided to remove her from the vehicle, and deputies took her into custody without further incident.

Jail records list felony charges including child neglect without great bodily harm and making a false report of planting a bomb. She also faces a misdemeanor charge of resisting arrest without violence.

Hurlburt Field is satellite of Eglin Air Force Base in the Florida panhandle and is home to Air Force Special Operations Command (AFSOC) and the 1st Special Operations Wing.

Likely not Åland.

events.title: Hackers have breached the U.S. Air Force's Cloud One, its cloud computing platform, according to a report from Reuters. The intrusion was di
events.description:
Hackers have breached the U.S. Air Force's Cloud One, its cloud computing platform, according to a report from Reuters. The intrusion was discovered within the past month or so during a system upgrade and has disrupted the platform. 

Cloud One hosts applications that manage Air Force personnel data, pay, logistics and maintenance, along with systems that track air defense radar feeds and munitions. 

Sources said migration of back office applications has been paused, updates to existing applications were blocked, and some users lost administrator rights. One source said the intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the platform's control plane, which could in theory give access to operational data such as aircraft status, though it is unclear whether they did. Cyber Command has been called in to assess the damage. The Air Force declined to comment on specific networks.

"you can search for videos of the Russian Arm
events.description:
Rybar complains about the 'near-complete absence of heavy drones' for logistics and strike.  

"you can search for videos of the Russian Armed Forces using heavy drones to supply assault troops. And compare their quantity with the stream of similar videos from the AFU, who had «Baba Yagas» back in 2022, and now they have become the basis of front-line logistics.

And this matters not only for offense, but also for defense. An assault trooper loses combat capability if he sits for months without food, ammunition and medicine. And only heavy drones and in part NRTK can deliver all this now.

Moreover, Vladimir Putin himself raised the problem a year ago. But even public attention and the president's directive did not become a reason to start mass-purchasing heavy drones"

CVE-2026-120705 OSGeo GeoServer XML Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-129243 OSGeo GeoServer Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability  CVE-2026-136716 Drupal Core Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions Vulnerability  These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterpr","content":"

CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-120705 OSGeo GeoServer XML Injection Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-129243 OSGeo GeoServer Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-136716 Drupal Core Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions Vulnerability 

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

events.title: Ce qui se passe avec l’important convoi maritime russe qui a quitté Baltysk il y a un mois est assez important pour attirer votre attention.
events.description:
Ce qui se passe avec l’important convoi maritime russe qui a quitté Baltysk il y a un mois est assez important pour attirer votre attention. 

En Octobre plusieurs navires sont identifiés à Baltysk en Russie en train de charger du matériel militaire sur plusieurs navires. 

Ces navires finissent par quitter la Russie et se diriger vers la mediterannée et vraisemblablement pour décharger en Libye, au profit d’Africa Corps. 

Finalement le navire de guerre russe Mercury est coulé à quai et un autre navire cargo sous pavillon russe au large de la Libye est frappé, et dans les deux cas par des drones maritimes. 

Et depuis, ces navires venus de Baltysk fond demi tour. 

Quoi qu’on en pense c’est assez fou d’observer cette guerre de l’ombre en temps réel.

events.title: Before NVIDIA’s Board of Directors announced earlier this week that it would be reinstating Jensen Huang as President and CEO, appearing to
events.description:
Before NVIDIA’s Board of Directors announced earlier this week that it would be reinstating Jensen Huang as President and CEO, appearing to be at the behest of President Trump and others at the White House; the Pentagon and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth were weighing the use of the 1950 Defense Production Act to force NVIDIA to restore Huang, three people familiar with the debate have told The Washington Post.

Hegseth and his senior deputy, Steve Feinberg, discussed how the DPA could be used as leverage to pressure NVIDIA’s Board of Directors to restore an executive to a company that they argued was critical to the national security of the United States. 

While the law provided no clear path to installing Huang back as CEO, it could be used as a warning. “Essentially they could use the DPA to force NVIDIA to shift more of its production to military projects,” said one of the three people, a member of the Trump Administration. Potentially curbing future production plans and profits of NVIDIA.

events.title: EXCLUSIVE: 🇷🇺🇱🇾 In a new joint investigation with @SONARROW_OSINT, we have identified a cargo transfer underway inside Benghazi port fol
events.description:
EXCLUSIVE: 🇷🇺🇱🇾 In a new joint investigation with @SONARROW_OSINT, we have identified a cargo transfer underway inside Benghazi port following the Ukrainian strike.

New Vantor satellite imagery from 26 November shows Russian cargo ship ASCALON moored alongside ANGARA, with cranes deployed over the holds and cargo apparently being transferred between the two vessels.

The imagery also shows:

🔹 🇷🇺 ASCALON general cargo ship, rafted alongside ANGARA with cranes deployed over the holds.
🔹 🇷🇺 ANGARA (IMO 9179842) container carrier.

🔹 🇷🇺 ANASTASIIA general cargo ship, moored at a nearby quay.

🔹 🇷🇺 MERKURY Steregushchiy-class corvette, sunk.

With ANGARA having been targeted in the attack, could ASCALON now be taking over the delivery of its cargo?  

We will keep monitoring.

@InsiderGeo × @SONARROW_OSINT

events.title: "Russia’s oil processing rates have plunged to the lowest in more than two decades as Ukraine continues to strike refineries, according to R
events.description:
"Russia’s oil processing rates have plunged to the lowest in more than two decades as Ukraine continues to strike refineries, according to Rystad Energy, heaping pressure on the country’s domestic fuel supplies.

Refinery runs totaled between 2.6 million and 2.7 million barrels a day as of Monday, roughly halving since Oct. 30, said Viktor Kurilov, a senior oil analyst at the research and intelligence firm. That has taken crude-processing rates back below multiyear lows seen during previous waves of attacks earlier this year."

events.title: Coast Guard’s updated Force Design plan includes Maven Smart System, other digital advancements
events.description:
The sea service is looking for tech that officials say will give the organization “decision advantage.”
The post Coast Guard’s updated Force Design plan includes Maven Smart System, other digital advancements appeared first on DefenseScoop.
events.raw_data:
{"source":"defensescoop","title":"Coast Guard’s updated Force Design plan includes Maven Smart System, other digital advancements","link":"https://defensescoop.com/2026/11/25/coast-guard-force-design-update-digital-modernization/","pubDate":"Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:55:50 +0000","contentSnippet":"The sea service is looking for tech that officials say will give the organization “decision advantage.” The post Coast Guard’s updated Force Design plan includes Maven Smart System, other digital advancements appeared first on DefenseScoop.","contentEncoded":"

The U.S. Coast Guard’s latest force design update includes the Maven Smart System AI tool that has been embraced by the Pentagon, among other digital modernization initiatives.

MSS, built by Palantir, can fuse disparate systems, data streams and intelligence information for commanders. It’s intended to help users make better and faster decisions.

The Coast Guard, which falls under the Department of Homeland Security but is considered a military service, noted its interest in the MSS platform as it pursues resilient command and control and faster mission workflows to achieve “decision advantage.”

The sea service “must drastically compress decision cycles and increase their accuracy,” officials wrote in a new report, “Force Design: Forging the Future,” that was released this month.

“Comprehensive integration of sensor data, intelligence, and operator input through the Tactical Awareness Kits (TAK), Maven Smart System, and enhanced mission workflows will integrate feeds to provide an operational reality with shared understanding. A digitally connected architecture empowers front line operators with decentralized autonomy to move at the speed of mission,” the document added.

Another initiative on the agenda is the fielding of Coastal Sentinel, a “system of systems” architecture that’s designed to boost maritime domain awareness by linking the service’s existing multi-modal and multi-domain sensors into a single, unified network, according to a Coast Guard description of the effort, which falls under the organization’s command, control, communications, computers, cyber/combat systems and intelligence portfolio. Along with sensor fusion, it involves tactical communications and networks, data engineering and management, analysis applications, and visualization and tasking tools.

The project will provide a “massive upgrade” to the Coast Guard’s C2 posture, according to the service.

“For personnel on the front line, this means background super intelligence automates data processing and integrates multi-agency feeds into a shared, real-time map,” officials wrote on a Coast Guard website, using the Trump administration’s preferred name for artificial intelligence. “It cuts out the clutter, spots threats instantly and gives Coast Guard men and women the exact information they need to make fast, decisive calls when lives and national security are on the line.”

According to the updated Force Design document, phase 1 development of Coastal Sentinel is slated to begin in fiscal 2027 at Sector San Diego, and additional sites will include the Houston-Galveston and Miami sectors. The service plans to implement the capability across multiple Coast Guard districts following the initial phase.

The service also intends to expand the rollout of Digital Seabag technology.

The Digital Seabag initiative provides service members with “dedicated, role-tailored mobile devices” that will streamline their work, according to a Coast Guard news release published earlier this month.

“Instead of waiting around for open workstations or dealing with slow, paper-based processes, crews can complete mission-critical tasks directly on scene, reclaiming hundreds of hours of administrative waste and returning them straight to frontline operations,” the news release stated.

More than 2,000 devices were deployed over the past year, and additional deliveries are expected across the fleet in the coming months. By March 2027, more than 8,000 boat force operators are expected to receive the tech, and a “service-wide” rollout to divers will give them access to a “Digital Dive Side” app that’s designed to streamline training management, safety notifications and gear checkouts, according to the news release.

The Coast Guard’s acquisition plans also include a variety of unmanned aerial systems and sea drones, among other assets.

The sea service’s modernization efforts have been boosted by $24.6 billion in funding that was provided to the organization via the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that was passed last year. Nearly $20 billion of that money pot has already been obligated, according to the Coast Guard.

However, additional infusions of funding to support modernization will be needed in the coming years.

“What the USCG needs now is enactment of the President’s budget request for [fiscal 2027] followed by increased, sustained top-line investment of $20 billion each year to operate, maintain, and support the new assets that are being delivered and acquire additional assets the USCG needs to meet the increased mission demands from the Nation,” officials wrote in the new Force Design report.

events.title: BREAKING: The Royal Air Force is moving aircraft to hangars and hardened shelters at night to protect them from possible drone threats, it i
events.description:
BREAKING: The Royal Air Force is moving aircraft to hangars and hardened shelters at night to protect them from possible drone threats, it is understood.

There are also plans to erect anti-drone nets around warplanes that remain exposed, such as by runways or at airbases that lack sufficient protection.

Such counter-drone netting is a common sight across Ukraine to help defend military equipment, critical national infrastructure and key roads from incoming Russian drones.

The moves by the RAF - also reported by @larisamlbrown @thetimes - are a clear indication of how the UK’s armed forces are strengthening their defences on the home front at a time of growing threats. ⬇️

events.title: CISA Adds 10 Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
events.description:
CISA has added 10 new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability
CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability 
CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability 
CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnera
events.raw_data:
{"source":"cisa","type":"advisory","title":"CISA Adds 10 Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog","link":"https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/11/25/cisa-adds-10-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog","pubDate":"Wed, 25 Nov 26 12:00:00 +0000","contentSnippet":"CISA has added 10 new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability  CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability  CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnera","content":"

CISA has added 10 new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability
  • CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab XML Injection Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab Weak Authentication Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab OS Command Injection Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab Not Failing Securely Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input Vulnerability 

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

events.title:
It is worth explaining why 720,000 russian military deaths over nearly five years of war matter much more than many think.

An ordinary russ
events.description:
It is worth explaining why 720,000 russian military deaths over nearly five years of war matter much more than many think.

An ordinary russian may not give a fuck about these 720,000 dead. Many would say, well, it was their choice. Some see it as tragic, some feel for them, but much of the general population appears indifferent.

A large proportion of these troops signed contracts voluntarily in exchange for money. There is a very different perception of their deaths in society. "Your choice, you knew the risks, you took them, and now you are dead. Sorry, but that's the way it is."

So let's look at recruitment numbers.

Russian budget data shows that the regional cost of recruiting a soldier increased by approximately 36% year over year in October, while recruitment fell by 11% over the first ten months of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025.

They are offering more but getting less. This is an obvious indicator of the exhaustion of their existing recruitment pools.

There are two main reasons why I think we are seeing this:

Information about losses becomes more accessible every day. More people lose family members, more wounded soldiers return home, and more soldiers tell their families what is actually happening on the battlefield. This information spreads through society.
The low-hanging fruit of recruitment is gradually disappearing. Those in financial desperation, those heavily in debt, highly motivated patriots, criminals and others for whom military service was an attractive option have already been heavily recruited.

Every new recruit costs more and is harder to get. The longer this continues, the more difficult recruitment becomes.

Fine, but russia still recruits large numbers of people and manages to fill gaps in its military rosters. That is correct.

events.title: Questions about DOD’s frontier AI organization linger after Trump-ordered rebrand and website redesign
events.description:
Experts urged the Pentagon to share more information about the SIO with the public, as the CDAO historically supplied.
The post Questions about DOD’s frontier AI organization linger after Trump-ordered rebrand and website redesign appeared first on DefenseScoop.
events.raw_data:
{"source":"defensescoop","title":"Questions about DOD’s frontier AI organization linger after Trump-ordered rebrand and website redesign","link":"https://defensescoop.com/2026/11/24/trump-ai-rebrand-pentagon-super-intelligence-office-sio/","pubDate":"Tue, 24 Nov 2026 22:31:15 +0000","contentSnippet":"Experts urged the Pentagon to share more information about the SIO with the public, as the CDAO historically supplied. The post Questions about DOD’s frontier AI organization linger after Trump-ordered rebrand and website redesign appeared first on DefenseScoop.","contentEncoded":"

Questions are swirling about recent reforms to the office that leads the Defense Department’s enterprise artificial intelligence deployments after a public rebrand and subsequent redesign that removed basic details about the team’s current priorities and organizational structure from the government website.

This week, Pentagon spokespersons declined to confirm the official serving as the Maven Smart System program director or describe other high-level positions inside the hub formerly known as the Chief Digital and AI Office, which was recently renamed as the Super Intelligence Office to match the second Trump administration’s ongoing push to replace government references to “AI” with “SI.”

“Reorganizing is normal, and every new team gets to put its own mark on the mission,” said Savan Kong, CEO and co-founder of AI startup Your Roster, who previously served as the DOD’s first-ever chief experience officer. “But who runs a program like Maven isn’t a minor detail.”

He and others told DefenseScoop that industry partners, Congress, and U.S. military personnel who depend on the office for algorithms and other in-demand frontier AI tools need to know who is accountable for their use inside the government.

“Being open about leadership during a transition builds trust,” Kong said. “Removing that information does the opposite, and it makes a hard transition even harder.”

These changes at the Pentagon’s one-stop AI shop follow an executive order issued by President Donald Trump in September, requiring all federal agencies to call artificial intelligence capabilities “super intelligence” in official correspondence, websites, reports and job titles. 

The president and his staff suggested that adopting SI as the official term would ensure the government is dedicated to maximizing and accelerating the technology to counter America’s adversaries advancing in the influential field.

However, this shift in terminology does not change existing U.S. regulations around AI without legislation from Congress. It also does not represent a new technological milestone. In academia and industry, “artificial superintelligence” typically refers to hypothetical future systems that exceed human-level general intelligence.

In a statement revealing the DOD’s shift from CDAO to SIO, Cameron Stanley, who oversees the office, said that this “redesignation is a clear signal of where the Department of War is going.” 

(Trump issued an executive order rebranding DOD as the DOW last year, though formally changing the agency’s name also requires an act of Congress.)

Stanley’s announcement indicated that the office’s existing operational programs, solicitations and partnerships will continue “uninterrupted under the new banner.” The transition, he said, would be rolling out across the department’s digital systems, enterprise applications and component headquarters in the near term.

Since then, the office has been iteratively changing the design and contents of its public-facing website, which was formerly AI.mil, and is now SI.mil. As of this week, the site’s “Leadership” landing page lists only two positions — Stanley’s and the principal deputy, Andy Mapes.

Unlike previous versions, the website no longer discloses any other positions or officials serving in the AI shop.

A source who requested anonymity to discuss the internal workings of the office this week told DefenseScoop that Army Col. Molly Solsbury is no longer the Maven Smart System program director inside the SIO. They also suggested that several other senior roles there are unfilled.

Built by Palantir Technologies and anchored under the SIO, the Maven Smart System is considered the Pentagon’s flagship AI-enabled software platform for command-and-control, battlefield awareness and complex intelligence fusion. 

MSS adoption and investments have been surging across the military this year, largely influenced by a directive from DOD leadership to mature the platform into a formal program of record.

Pentagon spokespersons did not directly respond to DefenseScoop’s questions regarding who is serving as the Super Intelligence Office’s program director for the Maven Smart System at this time, or confirm Army Col. Molly Solsbury’s current role. 

“Given the ever-increasing role AI plays in planning and executing military missions across the globe and how interwoven it is throughout our military networks, especially Maven, transparency is a must,” a former U.S. military official told DefenseScoop on Tuesday. “Without transparency, there’s a real risk of AI being misused or misapplied which could lead to a whole host of security concerns at home and abroad.”

Pentagon spokespersons also did not provide updated information this week about the office’s current organizational setup and leadership lineup, in the wake of the rebrand and digital redesign.

In an email on Monday, an individual who asked to be referred to as a War Department official told DefenseScoop: “Our organization routinely aligns personnel to meet operational requirements. We do not comment on individual assignments below the Senior Executive Service level.”

Regarding that response, sources also urged DOD to share more information about the SIO’s workforce and priorities with the public — as the CDAO historically supplied.

Virginia Burger, a senior defense policy analyst for the Project on Government Oversight’s Center for Defense Information, noted that the Maven platform is “a permanent, billion-dollar program” that more than 100,000 defense and military personnel use. 

“It’s the foundational software for military targeting. The department’s own memo said making Maven a program of record would create clear lines of accountability,” Burger, who served for almost a decade as an active-duty Marine Corps officer, told DefenseScoop. “If there’s been a leadership change, the Pentagon should say so.” 

In her view, “declining to confirm who runs the program while scrubbing the website of leadership details is the opposite of accountability.”  

Burger also noted that experts’ calls for transparency are emerging as “a new Congress prepares to ask hard questions about AI in targeting” after a U.S. Tomahawk missile strike reportedly hit an elementary school in Iran during Operation Epic Fury.

“The person in charge is the one who answers when something goes wrong. That’s the standard across the military. Transparency is how Congress and taxpayers make sure these systems work as promised and that someone is responsible when they don’t,” Burger said. “If the department doesn’t want to put that face forward, let’s hope senior leaders are willing to take the heat and answer the hard questions.”

events.title: Space Systems Command eyes mid-2028 for GPS sustainment upgrade contract
events.description:
The award would be the successor to the GPS Control Segment Sustainment II (GCS II) contract, won by Lockheed Martin.
The post Space Systems Command eyes mid-2028 for GPS sustainment upgrade contract appeared first on DefenseScoop.
events.raw_data:
{"source":"defensescoop","title":"Space Systems Command eyes mid-2028 for GPS sustainment upgrade contract","link":"https://defensescoop.com/2026/11/24/space-systems-command-gps-sustainment-upgrade-contract/","pubDate":"Tue, 24 Nov 2026 20:45:06 +0000","contentSnippet":"The award would be the successor to the GPS Control Segment Sustainment II (GCS II) contract, won by Lockheed Martin. The post Space Systems Command eyes mid-2028 for GPS sustainment upgrade contract appeared first on DefenseScoop.","contentEncoded":"

The Space Force has marked mid-2028 as the planned award window for next-generation GPS sustainment services under a five-year contract as it susses out potential capabilities with a new survey to industry. 

The service is looking for vendors that can simultaneously provide upkeep of traditional GPS ground systems and consistently tack on upgrades as modernized spacecraft come online, according to a Nov. 20 sources-sought notice. Industry responses are due Jan. 4. 

The Sustaining Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) and Integrating with Development to Enhance Readiness (SPIDER) award would be the successor to the follow-on GPS Control Segment Sustainment II (GCS II) contract, first handed to Lockheed Martin in 2019. A follow-on to that award was slated to wrap in 2025 but the Space Force added three option years to extend the performance term through 2028. 

“Lockheed Martin brings decades of experience modernizing and sustaining the GPS ground and space segments, ensuring warfighters and civilians worldwide can depend on resilient and reliable GPS capabilities. We plan to respond to the U.S. government’s sources sought notice request for information on the future sustainment of the GPS ground control system,” a Lockheed spokesperson told DefenseScoop.

The sources-sought notice states that SPIDER “represents a paradigm shift from pure hardware and software sustainment to a unified sustainment and continuous development integration model.”

The sustainment system should pair with next-generation satellites like the GPS III follow-on (GPS IIIF), the most capable upgraded constellation of satellites built by Lockheed. 

The contractor and the Space Force launched their 10th and last GPS III into space in April; the GPS IIIF will follow, which brings to the table triple the accuracy and eight times the anti-jamming strength, according to a Lockheed announcement. 

SPIDER must also oversee civil navigation signals and maintain resilience to electronic warfare and cyberattacks through consistent software upgrades, according to the notice. 

The award should take shape as a five-year indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) contract with another five-year optional ordering period. And, “due to the high complexity and mission-critical nature of the support,” the Space Force plans to award SPIDER through “multiple task orders to manage operational risk and baseline modernization,” the RFI states.

The notice calls for industry replies focused on any of six outlined target areas at control stations and monitoring stations across the country. The six “task areas” include:

  • Provide systems engineering help for constant GPS sustainment across the world
  • Seamless ground-segment hardware and software upgrade integrations
  • Hardware and software maintenance at control stations
  • Consistent monitoring of cyber threats
  • Integrated logistics support for ground systems
  • Manage government-furnished property (GFP) networks across sites 

Most of the work under the potential upcoming contract would take place at Schriever Space Force Base, Colorado, and Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, according to the RFI. 

Updated on Nov. 25, 2026, at 9:55 AM: This story has been updated to include comment from a Lockheed Martin spokesperson.

Since the full-scale invasion began, Norway has given Ukraine $16
events.description:
Norway has become one of the key defenders of Ukraine's skies. 🇺🇦🤝🇳🇴

Since the full-scale invasion began, Norway has given Ukraine $16.7 billion in security assistance. In 2026, it kept its support at the record level it first reached in 2025.

Norway is the largest contributor to PURL, which pays for Patriot missiles and other air defense assets. 

It was also Ukraine's largest partner in funding Ukrainian-made drones this year, and it trains more than 5,000 Ukrainian warriors every year.

Thank you, @Forsvarsdep!

Editor’s Note: Nand C. Bardouille, Ph.D., is the Founder and Executive Director of the Small States Observatory (SSO), an independent policy platform dedicated to advancing small state agency in an increasingly uncertain world.

By Richard Ponzio, Director, Global Governance, Justice & Security Program

“We are being drawn into a world dominated by power and less by the rule of law. So, who must speak for the Caribbean?”

This pointed question, posed by Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley at the recent launch of Sir Kenneth Hall’s Caribbean Integration: The Patterson Doctrine at The University of the West Indies Mona Campus, goes to the heart of a growing geopolitical dilemma confronting the Caribbean Community (CARICOM).

CARICOM is a regional grouping of 14 sovereign, primarily small island developing states in the Caribbean Basin. Since its establishment in 1973, CARICOM has sought to translate small state vulnerabilities into collective diplomatic strength. Except for Haiti, independent since 1804, the bloc’s sovereign members gained independence between the 1960s and 1980s. Foreign policy coordination has been central to that ambition.  

As reported by The Jamaica Gleaner on November 17, Mottley called for a political head of CARICOM, arguing that the bloc’s rotating six-month chairmanship was inadequate to provide continuity, articulate regional interests, and ensure implementation of collective decisions. Her intervention is timely, yet the challenge extends beyond CARICOM’s leadership arrangements. At issue is whether its Member States can preserve sufficient strategic coherence to exercise collective influence in an international environment increasingly shaped by great-power assertiveness and the weakening of rules-based multilateralism.

This predicament reinforces arguments I advanced in my recent IPI Global Observatory article, “CARICOM Has a Great-Power Problem,” and subsequently developed in my Oxford Review of Latin American Studies analysis, “Why CARICOM Is Caught in a Strategic Autonomy Trap.”

The reassertion of U.S. hemispheric power is exposing fundamental differences in how Caribbean governments calculate their strategic interests. Washington’s increasingly assertive posture has sharpened competing approaches to responding to U.S. power. Accommodation, hedging, and institutional or “soft” balancing, represent different strategies through which Caribbean governments seek to preserve room for independent action under conditions of profound asymmetry.

Such differences are not inherently problematic. CARICOM Member States have distinct economic dependencies, security relationships, and diplomatic priorities. Their exposure to American economic, security, and diplomatic pressure also varies, producing different calculations about the costs of dissent and the benefits of accommodation. The danger arises when these divergent national calculations undermine the bloc’s capacity to develop and sustain common diplomatic positions. What may appear rational from the standpoint of individual governments can collectively weaken CARICOM’s negotiating leverage.

The October 28 United Nations (UN) General Assembly vote calling for an end to the U.S. economic, commercial, and financial embargo against Cuba illustrates this predicament. Trinidad and Tobago voted against the resolution, while Guyana, Haiti, and Jamaica abstained. Three other CARICOM Member States did not record a vote. These approaches to the vote broke with the region’s long-standing pattern of broad support for the resolution (seven CARICOM Member States voted in favor.)

This fractured outcome revealed more than disagreements over Cuba. It exposed competing calculations about the costs of defending shared diplomatic principles, accommodating Washington, and preserving national room for maneuver.

The vote does not establish that every government’s position was determined by American pressure. Rather, it illustrates how an increasingly coercive geopolitical environment can intensify existing differences among states facing unequal external constraints.

Herein lies what I have termed CARICOM’s strategic autonomy trap: The same external pressures that make collective action more indispensable can simultaneously make regional cohesion more difficult to sustain. This paradox has important implications for Mottley’s proposed institutional remedy.

Her call for a political head capable of providing continuity beyond CARICOM’s rotating chairmanship addresses a genuine weakness in regional governance. Stronger leadership could improve diplomatic coordination, institutional follow-through, and the consistency with which Caribbean interests are represented internationally. But a stronger political center cannot, by itself, resolve disagreements over the principles and strategic priorities that should guide collective action. Its effectiveness would ultimately depend on Member States’ willingness to delegate meaningful authority, sustain agreed positions, and accept some of the political costs of collective action. Without these commitments, institutional reform risks strengthening the machinery of regional representation without strengthening the substance of collective agency.

The central question, therefore, is not simply who speaks for the Caribbean, but whether its governments can agree on what should be said, under what circumstances, and with what degree of collective commitment. This distinction matters because regional diplomatic influence is not produced by representation alone. It depends on the capacity to translate shared interests into coordinated positions, coordinated positions into consequential international engagement, and that engagement into sustained political leverage.

The challenge also extends beyond CARICOM’s internal arrangements. For small states, regional coordination and rules-based multilateralism are mutually reinforcing sources of influence. Regional cooperation aggregates otherwise limited diplomatic capabilities, while multilateral institutions provide mechanisms through which smaller countries can defend sovereign equality, shape international rules, and seek to constrain arbitrary exercises of power. The weakening of either diminishes the effectiveness of the other.

CARICOM’s fragmentation therefore carries consequences for its ability to influence wider debates about global governance reform. A region struggling to maintain common positions in response to external pressure risks finding its collective voice increasingly diminished in negotiations over the international institutions on which its strategic autonomy partly depends. These considerations are especially pertinent to discussions at the recently held T20 U.S. Summit 2026, where the relationship between the UN and the G20, global governance reform, and international cooperation featured prominently.

For Caribbean and other small states, the multilateral reform imperative must extend beyond questions of representation. It must also address the credibility, effectiveness, and authority of international institutions, and the conditions under which formal sovereign equality can translate into meaningful influence over decisions and outcomes.

Stronger multilateral institutions alone will not compensate for fragmented regional diplomacy. Small states must also strengthen their capacity to act collectively within those institutions, defend common priorities, and build coalitions capable of shaping international outcomes. The central paradox is stark: CARICOM needs collective agency and effective multilateralism most precisely when geopolitical pressures threaten to weaken both. Mottley’s warning should therefore prompt more than a debate about regional leadership structures. It demands a deeper reassessment of how CARICOM reconciles national strategic calculations with the collective interests that underpin its relevance in international affairs. Ultimately, the challenge is not merely to give CARICOM a stronger voice, but to ensure that it retains the strategic coherence and collective leverage necessary to make that voice consequential.

Summary

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code with webserver privileges.

The following versions of Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series are affected:

  • AK-SM8xxA <=5.4.0 (CVE-2026-129713)
CVSS Vendor Equipment
v3 9.8 Danfoss AK-SM8xxA
1 Vulnerability
Stack-based Buffer Overflow

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Commercial Facilities
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: Denmark

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-129713
A stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated CGI handler of the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controller allows remote attackers to send specially crafted HTTP/S POST requests, leading to memory corruption, webserver restart and hypothetically potential arbitrary code execution with webserver privileges. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.
Read More

1 Affected Product

Danfoss AK-SM8xxA <=5.4.0

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Mitigation
This vulnerability will be addressed in an upcoming Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series software release (version 5.5.x). In addition, Danfoss will remove the ability for users to disable Strict Mode in future software releases.

Mitigation
Until a software update is available, Danfoss recommends the following mitigations: * Follow the guidance provided in the product documentation and do not expose devices directly to the Internet or assign them public IP addresses. * Restrict remote access to affected devices by using a secure VPN or other protected network architecture. * Configure all affected devices to operate in Strict Mode, which provides enhanced security protections. * Use strong, unique passwords for all user accounts and administrative access. * For additional security recommendations and best practices see the Danfoss AK-SM 800 security guidance page: https://www.danfoss.com/en/service-and-support/downloads/dcs/adap-kool-software/ak-sm-800a/#tab-overview

Additional Metrics

Relevant CWE: CWE-121 Stack-based Buffer Overflow

CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String
3.1 9.8 CRITICAL CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H
4.0 9.3 CRITICAL CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N

View CVE Details

Acknowledgments

  • Carlo Meijer of Midnight Blue reported CVE-2026-129713 to CISA.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:

  • Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.
  • Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.
  • Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.

Summary

Schneider Electric is aware of a vulnerability in its EcoStruxure™ Power Build Rapsody product. CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability  CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability  CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability  These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks t","content":"

CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability 

  • CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability 

  • CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability 

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

View CSAF

Summary

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow attackers to corrupt application memory and cause instability or a crash, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution, if a user is convinced to open a malicious file.

The following versions of AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software are affected:

  • C-More EA9 Programming Software <=V6.80 (CVE-2026-127280)
CVSS Vendor Equipment
v3 7.8 AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software
1 Vulnerability
Heap-based Buffer Overflow

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Water and Wastewater Systems
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: United States

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-127280
C-More EA9 Programming Software V6.80 does not adequately validate data read from a project file before using it in heap memory operations. A crafted file causes a heap buffer overrun during file open, resulting in heap corruption and instability within the application. An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by convincing a user to open a malicious project file delivered through common distribution channels such as email, file sharing, or removable media.
Read More

1 Affected Product

AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software <=V6.80

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Vendor fix
Update C-More EA9 Programming Software to V6.81: https://www.automationdirect.com/support/software-downloads

Mitigation
If you cannot update to the latest software or firmware version right away, apply the following compensating controls to reduce risk until the update can be performed. These measures are temporary and do not replace the update, which remains the primary and recommended remediation. Apply these controls as appropriate based on the vulnerability, assessed risk, operational requirements, and characteristics of your environment. Implement changes under your established management-of-change process. Before implementing isolation, access-control, or network-configuration changes, evaluate potential impacts to safety, availability, and essential operational functions. • Isolate affected engineering workstations and OT systems from external and nonessential networks, including the internet and corporate IT networks, where operationally feasible. • Disable or tightly restrict vendor, contractor, and other remote access to the affected OT environment until the vulnerability can be remediated. Where remote access is operationally required, use a hardened jump host, enforce multi-factor authentication, apply least-privilege access, and limit access to authorized, time-bound sessions. • Use trusted, dedicated OT networks for device communication. Where practicable and appropriate to the assessed risk, use dedicated or physically separated infrastructure for higher-criticality systems. Where logical segmentation is used, ensure segmentation controls are appropriately configured, secured, and monitored. • Restrict both physical and logical access to affected systems to authorized personnel only. Apply least-privilege principles to administrative, engineering, maintenance, and service access. • Configure application allowlisting, where supported, so that only trusted and pre-approved applications are permitted to execute. Block unauthorized software. • Use appropriate antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools where supported and compatible with the affected system. Configure host-based and network firewalls to permit only required communications. • Disable unnecessary services, ports, protocols, and communication pathways associated with the affected systems. Where a service or protocol cannot be disabled for operational reasons, restrict access to trusted systems and authorized users wherever possible. • Enable and regularly review available system, security, and network logs to identify suspicious or unauthorized activity. Where appropriate, monitor communications to and from affected systems for unexpected connections or changes in network behavior. • Maintain secure, tested, and preferably offline backups of PLC programs, device configurations, engineering workstation configurations, and other information necessary to restore operations. Periodically verify that backups can be successfully restored. • Verify that critical OT functions can continue operating without unnecessary dependencies on external networks, cloud services, remote-access services, corporate IT services, or other nonessential systems. • If removable media is required to transfer files into an isolated or restricted environment, use controlled and trusted media and scan it for malicious content before use. • Continuously evaluate the risks associated with operating vulnerable or outdated firmware or software. Adjust compensating controls as the threat environment, operational requirements, or available vulnerability information changes. These compensating controls are intended to reduce exposure while remediation is pending. Organizations should prioritize applying the vendor-provided update as soon as it can be safely tested and deployed within the operational environment.

Additional Metrics

Relevant CWE: CWE-122 Heap-based Buffer Overflow

CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String
3.1 7.8 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H
4.0 8.4 HIGH CVSS:4.0/AV:L/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:A/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N

View CVE Details

Acknowledgments

  • rgod of TrendAI Zero Day Initiative reported this vulnerability to CISA.

 

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:

  • Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.
  • Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.
  • Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.

events.title: Marine Corps moving new chatbot prototyped at recent hackathon into full production
events.description:
The effort supports Marine Corps Community Services Connect, which was launched by the service as a new enterprise app.
The post Marine Corps moving new chatbot prototyped at recent hackathon into full production appeared first on DefenseScoop.
events.raw_data:
{"source":"defensescoop","title":"Marine Corps moving new chatbot prototyped at recent hackathon into full production","link":"https://defensescoop.com/2026/11/23/marine-corps-chatbot-hackathon-full-production/","pubDate":"Mon, 23 Nov 2026 22:41:58 +0000","contentSnippet":"The effort supports Marine Corps Community Services Connect, which was launched by the service as a new enterprise app. The post Marine Corps moving new chatbot prototyped at recent hackathon into full production appeared first on DefenseScoop.","contentEncoded":"

The Marine Corps hosted a “sprint hackathon” in California late last month, where dozens of military officials across nine teams competed to develop and refine artificial intelligence products that could quickly be released into the service for broader adoption and refinement.

Multiple teams that participated — including the “hackers” who ranked highest in the competition — generated AI-enabled tools to support Marine Corps Community Services, or MCCS, which aims to enhance the quality of life for Marines and their families.

One of those tools that came out on top is a new chatbot designed to help Marines and their families get on-demand answers and support, via the MCCS Connect mobile application, two officials involved told DefenseScoop in interviews last week. 

“They really were working through making it as user-friendly as possible, and that’s kind of the prompts that we kept giving them,” said Andrew Barcomb, MCCS digital product and user experience manager.

He shared new details about the hackathon-driven prototype and the organization’s plans to field it into broader production in the near term.

Broadly, MCCS provides programs and assets associated with morale, welfare, well-being, readiness and recreation to defense personnel across Marine Corps installations worldwide. Those elements help troops and retirees navigate military life, deployments, work transitions, physical fitness, off-duty activity options, and more.

Barcomb said MCCS Connect was launched as a new enterprise app to make information about these elements that can help enhance insiders’ life experiences more accessible around the Corps. 

For instance, he said the team behind it recently started building out a platform for small unit leaders to host in-app fitness challenges for Marines who are interested.

“They can make, like, scoreboards with each other — and talk shit to each other if they’re not stationed near each other. So, we’re trying to keep that community and that brotherhood that is the Marine Corps,” Barcomb said. “I’ve heard some Marines say it’s not the same as it used to be. Well, how do we get that back? How can we help facilitate the community and the connectedness that are the Marines?”

The Corps hosted its recent hackathon at the Naval Postgraduate School during the last week of October. The team leading it contacted Barcomb in the planning process, and MCCS efforts soon influenced some of the participants’ projects in the competition.

“We wanted to build an AI chatbot for our installation websites and MCCS Connect,” he explained. “So, we went out and gave them some use cases on what we wanted the chatbot to end up doing, and showed them some proof of concepts that we have been working on for the vision of where we want to go.”

Multiple teams made prototypes for MCCS over the course of the sprint. 

Barcomb said they worked through real-world use cases that would likely occur with the envisioned chatbot — like where to find childcare or local fitness facilities. All hackers involved prioritized setting appropriate safety guardrails and protection against AI hallucinations. 

In the process, they tested how chatbots should handle sensitive questions, including potential messages from Marines indicating suicidal thoughts.

“When someone goes and says they want to end it all, or they just bluntly say, ‘I want to kill myself,’ we’ve seen stories of how AI kind of hallucinates and almost like eggs them on to do it, unfortunately,” Barcomb said. “Whereas, we have guardrails where it doesn’t even get to the processing point of letting the AI respond. The check happens, and it just goes directly to content that is specifically written and curated by our suicide prevention staff — clinical people that have gone through and written this content that is very specific worded a certain way.”

Ultimately, one of the teams that created an MCCS Connect chatbot won the overall hackathon.

Post-hackathon, Barcomb is set to review that prototype and identify production requirements with the Marine Corps’ Operation StormBreaker team. StormBreaker is an enterprise DevSecOps platform that MCCS built and operates to move software capabilities across the force from development through deployment and sustainment.

“We’re working to collapse the tech valley of death,” Dave Raley, USMC chief digital services officer who leads Operation StormBreaker, told DefenseScoop. “Because we happen to have that capability, and we want to operationalize as quickly as possible what was done in the hackathon.”

He and Barcomb emphasized that, as they explore next steps, MCCS also wants direct feedback from Marines about how to make the app better serve their needs. The latter said he reviews every piece of input submitted through the MCCS Connect’s contact form.

“I want to know what people want in it — what struggles they’re having that an app can solve,” Barcomb said. “If somehow we can make technology work for them, I genuinely want to hear that.”

Washington, D.C. — Jupiter Huang, a 2025-2026 Junior Fellow at the Stimson Center, has been named a 2027 Rhodes Scholar. He is one of just 32 young scholars from the U.S. to receive this year’s prestigious Oxford University scholarship to promote leadership, service, and international understanding.

Huang served as a Junior Fellow with the Stimson Center’s South Asia Program, an elite fellowship for recent graduates focused on security and international policy related to South Asia. During his time at Stimson, he helped grow the Strategic Learning initiative, a signature Stimson project that provides free, online learning resources for students and professionals on strategic military and nuclear security issues in Southern Asia. His work was essential to expanding the range of online learning products beyond online courses, incorporating a podcast, explainer articles, and short-form content to bring Stimson’s expertise directly to viewers in a volatile region. He also authored publications on the strategic use of drones and air defense in South Asia.

“From its founding, the Stimson Center has fostered young thinkers and doers as they pursue solutions to the world’s toughest challenges,” said Stimson Center Acting President and CEO Rachel Stohl. “We are proud of Jupiter’s dedication to making the world safer and more secure, and excited to follow his journey as a Rhodes Scholar.”

Huang’s interest in the intersection of technology and nuclear security has been a throughline of his academic career. He graduated from Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service in 2025 with a degree in science, technology, and international affairs, where he also pursued an accelerated master’s degree in nuclear policy and emerging technology. He is currently a fellow at the National Nuclear Security Administration, focusing on how technological advances are changing the dynamics of global conflicts.

The South Asia Program Junior Fellowship gives highly talented recent graduates the opportunity to contribute to research, engagements, and outreach, while benefiting from mentorship and networking with think tank, academic, and government contacts. Former fellows have gone on to positions in across the U.S. government, leading think tanks, and top PhD and professional degree programs. Many have continued to focus on South Asia and security studies in their careers, directly contributing to the next generation of scholarship and thought leadership on these critical issues.

“Stimson’s Junior Fellows program gives young scholars a front-row seat to the diverse perspectives and policy priorities of a dynamic and strategically important region in a way few other early-career experiences can,” said Elizabeth Threlkeld, Director of the South Asia Program at the Stimson Center. “Jupiter’s energy, passion, and academic accomplishments are a testament to this model of support for the next generation of scholars shaping global security.”

As a Rhodes Scholar, Huang plans to pursue a PhD in international relations at Oxford, researching how commercial technology, and the non-governmental actors who control it, can escalate global conflicts. His research will explore how we can manage these risks and pursue strategies to more productively engage the technology sector on critical nuclear security issues.

About the Stimson Center

The Stimson Center promotes international security, shared prosperity, and justice through applied research and independent analysis, deep engagement, and policy innovation.

For three decades, Stimson has been a leading voice on urgent global issues. Founded in the twilight years of the Cold War, the Stimson Center pioneered practical new steps toward stability and security in an uncertain world. Today, as changes in power and technology usher in a challenging new era, Stimson is at the forefront: Engaging new voices, generating innovative ideas and analysis, and building solutions to promote international security, prosperity, and justice.


More at www.stimson.org.

events.description:

{"source":"defensescoop","title":"DISA boss highlights need for training, standardization to prepare for new era of ZT and AI-enabled cyber warfare","link":"https://defensescoop.com/2026/11/23/ai-cyber-warfare-zero-trust-lt-gen-stanton/","pubDate":"Mon, 23 Nov 2026 19:39:31 +0000","contentSnippet":"“If we don't standardize our architecture, we won't be able to drive at the speed required to meet the changing operating environment,” Lt. Gen. Paul Stanton said. The post DISA boss highlights need for training, standardization to prepare for new era of ZT and AI-enabled cyber warfare appeared first on DefenseScoop.","contentEncoded":"

The U.S. military must ensure it has the right training and architectures in place to operate effectively in an era of zero trust and AI-enabled cyber operations, the head of the Defense Information Systems Agency and Department of Defense Cyber Defense Command said Friday.

The Pentagon and the military services face a self-imposed deadline to reach “target level” ZT maturity by the end of fiscal 2027.

“The risk that that commander is taking [in sharing data] has to be isolated to that commander’s purview. And if you’re going to cross a unit boundary inside of the operating environment, there have to be control mechanisms and control measures that are inherent to the design. Guess what? Zero trust supports it when it’s properly implemented. Micro segmentation, full visibility of the data, policy enforcement points that all support the control necessary to make those decisions,” Army Lt. Gen. Paul Stanton, director of DISA and commander of DCDC, said at the Annual Data Forum, presented by AFCEA International.

“I can tell you, as the person responsible for defending SIPRNet, I am not going to allow a corps commander’s dirty data to traverse into the SIPRNet environment. However, we’re going to architect the environment that allows the corps commander to make a risk-informed decision, and then the data that traverses back out of his area of responsibility into the broader SIPRNet will cross the security appliance, so that we have confidence that it’s not extending the risk to the rest of the community. When you design the architecture that way, it affords you the dynamic decision-making necessary to support battlefield … speed and effectiveness by design,” he added.

Having the right architecture in place to boost information sharing among military forces while protecting security is necessary but insufficient, Stanton said, noting that having well-trained personnel is also critical.

“Anybody actually operate a zero-trust environment?” the DISA boss said. “You’re actually configuring the SD WAN appliance, you’re configuring the next-gen firewall, you’re configuring in the policy enforcement point, you’re driving the micro segmentation. … How easy is it? … It’s non-trivial. You got to train the force in order to be able to operate the weapons platform.”

He added: “Dropping a highly complex zero-trust operating environment onto a combatant command, expecting them to be able to properly orient the control mechanisms to support the dynamic nature of the fight and get the right data to the right place at the right time, is a dream if you don’t build the training mechanisms associated with the organization responsible for operating the system. Can’t separate that. We’re building it in parallel so that we have trained and ready forces prepared to operate the environment.”

Meanwhile, threats posed by AI-enabled cyberattacks are growing.

“Super intelligence,” which is the Trump administration’s preferred name for artificial intelligence, is an “accelerant poured onto everything for which we are responsible,” Stanton said.

The Defense Department must automate configuration changes and conduct defensive cyber operations “agentically” or else it won’t be able to keep pace with adversaries who use AI to carry out cyberattacks, he noted.

But if the DOD doesn’t decrease the complexity of its operating environment, it won’t be able to automate its configuration changes, Stanton warned.

“If you automated a configuration change in the environment that you’re currently responsible for, what would happen? Let your mind wander for a second,” he told the audience at Friday’s conference. “And if you think about the second- and third-order effects of that configuration change in the warfighting domain for which we are responsible, the consequences are non-trivial. We have to be able to automate. We have to be able to employ agentic capabilities, but we have to have the visibility to align with the control. If we don’t standardize our architecture, we won’t be able to drive at the speed required to meet the changing operating environment.”

On the sidelines of the conference, Stanton told DefenseScoop that the recent Hugging Face incident — which reportedly involved AI models developed by OpenAI that went rogue and breached a Hugging Face data pipeline during internal testing — was “eye-opening” for people who work in cybersecurity and cyber defense.

“I think that it 100% reinforced the approach that we’re driving at the Department of War to ensure our current security and future security as the speed, scope, and scale of adversarial SI-enabled activity continues to come up with new approaches like what happened in Hugging Face,” he said, using the Trump administration’s preferred name for the Department of Defense. “I recognize that Hugging Face was not intentionally nefarious, but you can imagine if [that type of technology] fell into the wrong hands.”

Stanton indicated that the Pentagon doesn’t need to develop separate defensive measures specifically geared toward thwarting threats posed by commercially developed AI models that go rogue.

“The good news side of the story is frankly it doesn’t matter if it was intentional or not. The defenses to prevent a system that is SI enabled gaining access into the environment are consistent,” Stanton told DefenseScoop.

events.title: Destroying Russian Forces, Disrupting Enemy Logistics and Improving Communications: Yevhen Lasiychuk Outlines the 7th Air Assault Corps’ Ope
events.description:
Destroying Russian Forces, Disrupting Enemy Logistics and Improving Communications: Yevhen Lasiychuk Outlines the 7th Air Assault Corps’ Operations in the Huliaipole Sector

Brigadier General Yevhen Lasiychuk, Commander of the 7th Air Assault Corps, held a meeting with American military analyst Michael Kofman @KofmanMichael.

Yevhen Lasiychuk summed up several months of the corps’ work in the Huliaipole direction. During this period, the 7th Air Assault Corps not only managed to establish effective command and control of units within its area of responsibility but also improved communication between brigades, particularly through the DELTA situational awareness system. This helped significantly increase the effectiveness of combat operations.

According to the Commander of the 7th Air Assault Corps, the effectiveness of engaging detected enemy targets has increased by 20% using the same set of forces and assets. 

Despite the enemy tripling the number of assault operations last month, units under the operational command of the 7th Air Assault Corps continue to hold back Russian forces and inflict significant losses on the occupying army. Over the past month, Ukrainian defenders in the Huliaipole sector killed or wounded nearly 2,900 Russian troops. They also struck 960 vehicles and motorcycles.

Another key area of effort is disrupting the logistics supporting the Russian grouping in Huliaipole. Units operating within the 7th Air Assault Corps’ area of responsibility systematically strike routes that are critical to the occupying forces, including bridges and crossings.

CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal Vulnerability

  •  CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.
