events.description:
2026 has been an exceptionally bad year for Russia. Just to recap:

- Russian forces lost occupied territory in parts of Donbas, while offensive operation in Kupyansk failed
- Hundreds of transport and tanker ships were damaged or destroyed in Azov and Black Sea
- Russian military casualties reached record levels, despite small or even in some cases negative net territorial gains.
- The road section of Crimean Bridge has been destroyed and Crimea is almost isolated 
- Ukrainian strikes have severely disrupted Russia's oil-refining industry
- Wildberries, one of Russia's largest companies and logistics provider has lost its warehouse infrastructure  
- Russia has lost numerous military aircraft, including bombers and fighter jets
- Oil export and seaport infrastructure has being severely damaged in Black, Azov and Baltic Sea’s 
- Russian air defenses have being severely degraded across Russia 
- Dozens of missile, electronics and defense-industrial production facilities were hit across Russia.

events.title: 🚀 Since 2022, startups and scale-ups such as @Xbow, @ursamajortech, and @anduriltech have entered a Western solid rocket motor market that
events.description:
🚀 Since 2022, startups and scale-ups such as @Xbow, @ursamajortech, and @anduriltech have entered a Western solid rocket motor market that until recently rested on a handful of incumbents in Europe and North America, notably @L3HarrisTech, Nammo, and Roxel.

Whether this is actually diversifying the supplier base depends on solid rocket motor qualification, the supply chains into which new suppliers are integrated, and the timelines for doing so.

My latest Missile Matters post maps Western solid rocket motor suppliers, the missile systems each supplies or targets, and the status of capacity expansions. It also identifies the major interceptor and strike programs that still depend on a single motor supplier.

Find the full post here
https://missilematters.substack.com/p/slow-burn-diversifying-the-western

events.title: Army plans to work with OpenAI on Project Gatekeeper
events.description:
Acting CIO Gabe Chiulli provided an update Friday on the Army’s cybersecurity efforts.
The post Army plans to work with OpenAI on Project Gatekeeper appeared first on DefenseScoop.
events.raw_data:
{"source":"defensescoop","title":"Army plans to work with OpenAI on Project Gatekeeper","link":"https://defensescoop.com/2026/11/20/army-project-gatekeeper-openai-gabe-chiulli/","pubDate":"Fri, 20 Nov 2026 22:49:30 +0000","contentSnippet":"Acting CIO Gabe Chiulli provided an update Friday on the Army’s cybersecurity efforts. The post Army plans to work with OpenAI on Project Gatekeeper appeared first on DefenseScoop.","contentEncoded":"

The Army plans to work with OpenAI as it moves forward with a new initiative to accelerate the accreditation process for commercial vendors looking to offer their software to the military, according to the service’s chief information officer.

Project Gatekeeper, which was unveiled last month, aims to automate the traditionally burdensome authority to operate (ATO) process, which often stretches on for months, allowing commercial vendors instead to submit code to an Army DevSecOps platform for quick validation.

“What Gatekeeper was all about was taking that same experience that we built on the DSO platform, bring it to a commercialized space and say, hey, we’ll get you that first initial vetting that says you get the green check mark, that you are actively good enough for our networks. Get their code through, and then that kind of alleviates that relationship barrier between industry that doesn’t have a relationship with the government,” Acting CIO of the Army Gabe Chiulli said Friday at the Annual Data Forum, presented by AFCEA International.

“They get the government check, and that code gets moved into an IL5 environment after it gets through all the different checks, and says, ‘hey, you are now capable of essentially selling your product or distributing your product into a secure Army enclave,’” Chiulli added.

He said he’s working with the other military department CIOs to try to establish “reciprocity” so that they don’t have to build their own systems for this type of process.

Vendors with a Defense Department Common Access Card can log in to Gatekeeper to use the system. But, Chiulli noted, officials are working to open it up more widely and allow companies to access it via the Login.gov platform.

At Friday’s conference, DefenseScoop asked the Army CIO about the timeline for integrating AI models into the Gatekeeper initiative.

“I’m going to put it into the next quarter,” Chiulli replied.

“I think what it’ll be is a phased approach of different commercialized models. So remember, this is on the commercial internet. The first phase of this was always meant to be that we were going to work with OpenAI in the first phase because … we’re using something like Login.gov. It helps us do the validation” using tools like OpenAI’s Daybreak, he said.

The Army wants to be cautious about how it releases an AI model vetting process into the DevSecOps pipeline, he noted.

“So, the first phase is working with OpenAI to kind of work through, like, what do we want to check first? Because there’s a lot of good tooling out there that does validation checks on software already, so we don’t want to repeat and just use tokens just for tokens purposes. We want to apply it in the most strategic, smart, intelligent way,” Chiulli said.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday.

After the first phase, the Army will likely start opening it up to other open source and commercial model providers, Chiulli said.

He noted that he’ll encourage companies to bring their own API keys.

“When you think about code scanning in an API era in a vulnerability scanner, it’s going to have logs on their code. So we want to make sure that they’re the only ones that can see that … from that perspective. So that is a protective kind of way we’re thinking through this so that, you know, as they bring their own API key they’re paying for that security from their perspective,” Chiulli said.

“We’ll do a call out at some point to … request different ways and different harnesses, if you will, for checking different things,” he added.

events.title: GAO calls for broad munitions plan, better data management from Pentagon
events.description:
Solving munitions shortages will be difficult without an overarching plan, authorities and better inventory oversight, a Government Accountability Office report warns. 
The post GAO calls for broad munitions plan, better data management from Pentagon appeared first on DefenseScoop.
events.raw_data:
{"source":"defensescoop","title":"GAO calls for broad munitions plan, better data management from Pentagon","link":"https://defensescoop.com/2026/11/20/gao-pentagon-munitions-plan-data-management/","pubDate":"Fri, 20 Nov 2026 18:25:19 +0000","contentSnippet":"Solving munitions shortages will be difficult without an overarching plan, authorities and better inventory oversight, a Government Accountability Office report warns. The post GAO calls for broad munitions plan, better data management from Pentagon appeared first on DefenseScoop.","contentEncoded":"

The Defense Department’s lack of long-term munitions foresight and spotty tracking of inventory data may hamper its ability to revive key munitions shortages amplified by the Iran war, a congressional watchdog report says. 

The Pentagon needs a sweeping plan to meet its goal of leveling up low munitions inventories, and while the department has set up certain processes and procedures, “it is not positioned to address these gaps,” an unclassified version of a September Government Accountability Office report, published Thursday, says. 

The department’s data tool for tracking munitions inventories, the Munitions Readiness Initiative (MRI), also suffers from inconsistent check-ups and is absent a data management plan, according to the report. The tool pulls from 37 data sources and is designed to consolidate service-specific munitions metrics for senior leaders in real time. 

“They haven’t routinely had a formal process for going back and ensuring that the data is correct or up to date,” Diana Moldafsky, director of defense capabilities and management at GAO, told DefenseScoop. 

While she declined to provide specific examples, the check-ins take place “on a really ad hoc basis and we’d find a few instances where there’d be discrepancies between the services and MRI,” she added. 

The report suggests setting up “consistent reconciliation” of data between the Office of the Undersecretary for Acquisition and Sustainment and the services to ensure leaders make decisions based on accurate numbers, which aligns with the Defense Department’s guidance for managing data. 

“We used basically the department’s own criteria, their data guidebooks to develop this recommendation,” Moldafsky said. “So they recognize that they should be doing this.”

The report also recommends the secretary of defense draw up a plan to restock key munitions and meet inventory needs in the long run, as well as hand authorities to one office to oversee the munitions revival.

Without a centralized plan, the department is “reactive to global events,” running the risk of pouring dollars into specific near-term requirements while overlooking shortages across the board, the report notes. 

The Army’s surge in 155 millimeter artillery shells, for example, addressed service-specific shortages but wasn’t driven by total munitions requirements, according to GAO. 

“Everybody is operating in kind of a vacuum of the closest need that we need to deal with now without considering how that need matches up with all of our other requirements and industrial base needs,” Moldafsky said. 

The Defense Department mostly agreed with GAO’s recommendations, although it pushed back on the report’s recommendation that the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO) — recently renamed the Super Intelligence Office (SIO) — should oversee the data management plan, according to written comments from August that addressed a draft of the report. 

That role should fall to the Office of the Undersecretary for Acquisition and Sustainment instead, according to the Pentagon’s replies. GAO agreed, although the report adds that SIO should have a hand in the plan. 

The Pentagon previously acknowledged a need to boost production capacity to fix shortages in several key munitions, according to June 2025 testimony from Steven Morani, who was serving as acting assistant defense secretary for sustainment at the time. The Iran war has only amplified the problem, the GAO report says.  

“This is a very tough effort and it requires a lot of prioritization, so you need to have a strategy to guide a department-wide solution, or I think they’ll have a tough time actually accomplishing any of their goals and addressing any of the shortages that they currently have,” Moldafsky said.

CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. 

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. 

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. 

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

events.title: Army extends ADOC pilot by a year as officials work to make the data ops center a more permanent fixture
events.description:
The Army Data Operations Center first went live as a task force in April under an initial six-month pilot effort.
The post Army extends ADOC pilot by a year as officials work to make the data ops center a more permanent fixture appeared first on DefenseScoop.
events.raw_data:
{"source":"defensescoop","title":"Army extends ADOC pilot by a year as officials work to make the data ops center a more permanent fixture","link":"https://defensescoop.com/2026/11/19/army-extends-data-operations-center-pilot/","pubDate":"Thu, 19 Nov 2026 22:20:27 +0000","contentSnippet":"The Army Data Operations Center first went live as a task force in April under an initial six-month pilot effort. The post Army extends ADOC pilot by a year as officials work to make the data ops center a more permanent fixture appeared first on DefenseScoop.","contentEncoded":"

The Army Data Operations Center pilot effort has been extended 12 months, giving senior leaders more time to decide whether to formalize the organization on a long-term basis.

The ADOC first went live as a task force in April under an initial six-month pilot effort aimed at helping help the Army tackle its data management challenges.

“What the ADOC highlighted on really day one is that we also have a data access problem, and so that’s what the ADOC is really chartered to do, and it’s to tackle the access to data, handle those data connection requests, and ensure that if we have soldiers or leaders or commanders or anyone for that matter who is looking for data that resides on another plane or behind another security boundary, … we’re going to knock that boundary down,” Col. Reginald “Reggie” Evans, director of the task force, said Thursday during a panel at the Annual Data Forum, produced by AFCEA International.

“The challenge that we have today is we have put more data into the hands of our soldiers than we ever have before, and so we’re talking from a theater Army headquarters all the way down to the soldier. That’s where you’re going to start to see the gaps and seams, and that’s where the ADOC is going to really make its money, and … why we need to be tied to the warfighter,” Evans said.

The organization created a ticketing system that enables it to field requests for assistance from units around the world.

The task force has leaned on artificial intelligence capabilities to facilitate its work.

“With the small team that we’ve had, automation and agentic workflows were critical,” Chad Nash, deputy of the ADOC, said during Thursday’s panel. “We were able to take a flow or a process that … was not documented [and] we were able to build in workflows that autonomously do agentic AI. We were able to build those fields and those forms to take that burden … off the soldier, off the warfighter, that administrator.”

The pilot effort has been extended until Oct. 1, 2027, according to Nash.

“What that will allow us to do is to continue gathering our findings and continue to allow us to gain metrics on what we’re seeing in volume of, you know, scale in terms of the challenges and those stovepipes that we may have. We’re also realizing some of the benefits of being able to solve these issues in [less] duration of time. Things that took in the beginning maybe two months to solve, we’re able to solve those problems in days,” he said.

After the extension period, Army leaders can make the decision on the long-term plan for the ADOC.

“We anticipate that,” Nash said. “And we’re only learning more, we’re only getting better, and certainly as we solve these tactical challenges, we’re evolving our processes, and in some instances, actually creating new processes using technology to make those things better.”

Evans suggested that takeaways from the initial pilot period have helped officials flesh out what a more permanent ADOC might like look.

“Over the last six months, we’ve learned what the structure looks like. We learned what roles, responsibilities and functions the ADOC should execute. We know what skill sets we need within the ADOC to execute those functions. We’ve identified a rough order of magnitude of what it would cost us. And so we’re taking all of that to our Army senior leaders for a decision to go ahead and move forward with formalizing ADOC. That would be our recommendation,” he said.

However, there are “longer lead items” and “action items” that still need to be worked through to enable that formalization, he added.

“There are some command plan actions that really take time, and so we just needed more time to get those actions in place so that at the end of this next 12 months, we can permanently fill those billets with folks versus the borrowed manpower that we’re using now,” Evans said.

events.title: Decoding Nepal’s Latest Disaster: A Multi-Hazard Puzzle in the Budhi Gandaki Basin
events.description:
A rapid scientific assessment of Nepal’s October 2026 extreme flow event, based on remote sensing analysis and research conducted on the ground immediately following the event.
The post Decoding Nepal’s Latest Disaster: A Multi-Hazard Puzzle in the Budhi Gandaki Basin appeared first on Stimson Center.
events.raw_data:
{"source":"stimson","title":"Decoding Nepal’s Latest Disaster: A Multi-Hazard Puzzle in the Budhi Gandaki Basin","link":"https://www.stimson.org/2026/decoding-nepals-latest-disaster-a-multi-hazard-puzzle-in-the-budhi-gandaki-basin/","pubDate":"Thu, 19 Nov 2026 20:04:42 +0000","contentSnippet":"A rapid scientific assessment of Nepal’s October 2026 extreme flow event, based on remote sensing analysis and research conducted on the ground immediately following the event. The post Decoding Nepal’s Latest Disaster: A Multi-Hazard Puzzle in the Budhi Gandaki Basin appeared first on Stimson Center.","contentEncoded":"

Just before 4:30 AM on October 11, 2026, people in the upper reaches of the Budhi Gandaki watershed in Nepal’s Gorkha district felt the earth shake and ran from their homes. People living along the river in the lower Tsum Valley said they heard and felt something that seemed like a massive landslide or avalanche coming, and minutes later, stones and dust rained down on their roofs in the dark. Over the next two hours, a terrifying series of debris flows came down the Budhi Gandaki River, sweeping away an estimated 121 homes in settlements along the riverbanks. The disaster also damaged bridges and hydropower projects throughout the watershed, and six people are still reported missing.

In the wake of this event, people across Nepal — still reeling from the trauma of the unprecedented Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster of late August and then a wave of storm-triggered flooding and landslides nearby in Gandaki Province toward the end of September — wondered out loud: Is this the new normal?

The Stimson team once again conducted a rapid post-disaster assessment, working closely with disaster managers and technical experts from the Government of Nepal to try to figure out what happened, how, and why. We analyzed remote sensing data and satellite imagery, examined locally generated content shared on social media, reviewed drone survey data collected by our government counterparts, and visited the most-impacted areas to conduct three days of on-the-ground field research. Ten days later, we felt we finally understood the complex hazard interactions and processes that shaped this event, the multi-episodic patterns of flow propagation that resulted, and the ways local people responded to this disaster.

As extreme flow events repeatedly occur across the Himalayan region, experts and planners are doing their best to improve risk assessment techniques to keep up with rapidly evolving patterns of disaster risk. While the Budhi Gandaki disaster was, thankfully, nowhere near as deadly or devastating as the horrifying Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster, it is a) still a very large and destructive multi-hazard event that justifies focused inquiry, b) yet another wake-up call that highlights the need to reassess settlement planning and infrastructure development in the face of chronic patterns of exposure and c) part of a broader and deeply worrying pattern. Understanding this unique and incredibly offers another piece of the broader puzzle as we, collectively, work to make sense of changing patterns of disaster risk.

This issue brief — the public version of a report we created for our Government of Nepal partners — summarizes our findings and offers a handful of recommendations to improve disaster-risk management policies and protocols. Along the way, this piece also outlines the multimodal approach our team used to make sense of this complex multi-hazard event, which we hope offers methodological insights that will be useful to others conducting forensic analyses of future disasters

Key Takeaways

Before diving into the details of our analysis, we would like to provide a brief overview of a few of the key findings emerging from this assessment:

  1. This cascading disaster unfolded as a multi-episodic event, instead of a single massive flow like the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster. It was experienced as a series of distinct flows that propagated in pulses or waves — which is a big reason why casualties were mercifully limited during this event. Impacted communities reported both a series of flood pulse events and rapid fluctuations in the level of the river over a period of over two hours. Deviations between patterns of observed flows along the river course indicate that both the Syar Khola and the larger Budhi Gandaki River were blocked by landslide and debris dams at multiple points, and that these dams failed, triggering the debris flows that caused the majority of damage downstream.

  2. The initial high-elevation slope failure is best characterized as a rock avalanche, or simply a landslide, and did not include as much glacial material as most analysts initially anticipated. The initial failure that initiated the Budhi Gandaki disaster seems to have mostly been rock. Critically, because the percentage of ice/snow included in the early stages was lower, the water content of the rock avalanche landslide and the subsequent hyper-concentrated flow was also lower. This is likely a major reason why the initial flow didn’t move as fast or propagate as far as it could have if more ice had been included — and why the initial flow instead behaved more like a dry landslide. This is critical because, conversely, more ice could have led to greater loss and damage.

  3. The largest debris flow, which caused the majority of damage downstream, was caused by the failure of a landslide/debris dam created below the confluence of the Syar and Budhi Gandaki, which breached just before 6:00 AM NPT. As we discovered (and describe in detail below), the largest and most devastating debris flow occurred due to the creation and subsequent failure of a landslide dam that blocked the Budhi Gandaki River (further downstream than most post-disaster analysts had realized). Local eyewitnesses in the area around this dam report that it began to drain just before 6:00 AM NPT and drained over a period of over 20 minutes, and this correlates with both downstream observations and the pulses recorded in the seismic data (see Fig 2).

  4. The multi-episodic nature of this event created more lead time for downstream communities and more opportunities for localized information sharing and alerting. While several riverine settlements were partially destroyed, the loss of human life was minimal, and many people did receive some kind of warning — from locals or authorities, though mostly the former. Again, the most devastating impacts to downstream communities were caused by debris flows that occurred between 90 and 120 minutes after the initial slope failure. This meant that people had more time to react, evacuate, and share and receive alerts. And after witnessing the unthinkable devastation caused by the August disaster, people reported that they ran to high ground faster than ever before.

  5. Patterns of exposure and vulnerability along the river corridor were remarkably different than in the case of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster. The total number of people exposed to this disaster in the Budhi Gandaki was also lower than in the August event because the overall pattern of development along the river corridor was different. Road development was in its earlier stages along most of the river course, hydropower projects were in the earlier phases of development, and most settlements were still located high above the river level. That said, plans for more intensive development in the area were in the works, and this event may lead to some rethinking, as yet another “wake-up call” to improve development planning in river corridors.

  6. Multimodal and interdisciplinary analysis is critical for this kind of rapid forensic analysis — and that includes qualitative analysis of local observations. Decoding the complex sequence of events that shaped this disaster required interpreting and integrating multiple different kinds of data, including: hydrological and seismic data, satellite imagery, drone footage, photographic and video evidence collected during the event, local testimonies collected during fieldwork, and our own observation of physical conditions on the ground. In this case, local accounts helped us gather critical pieces of the puzzle that helped us map out the multi-episodic pattern of propagation, understanding the timing, duration, and intensity of flows. In a broader sense, both disaster managers and scientists need to rethink the ways localized observations are collected and redesign information infrastructures to be able to make good use of local data.

  7. Post-disaster assessment protocols and workflows can be improved to help authorities make sense of complex events, using techniques like those we used here to triangulate between data sources — it just requires a focus on co-design and practice. Effective coordination between government organizations, scientific experts, and local disaster-risk managers is critical to increase the efficacy and accuracy of rapid post-disaster analyses. As Nepal and other Himalayan nations work to understand changing risks and prepare for future disasters, authorities need to also develop and refine post-event workflows for analyzing hazard processes and examining extant risks. Organizations like Stimson must work closely with government officials and technical partners in countries like Nepal to help build capacity for multimodal post-event analysis and protocols for rapid post-disaster assessment able to capture the nuance critical to understanding these complex multi-hazard events.

Deconstructing the Cascading Hazard Chain

The Budhi Gandaki disaster began with a high-elevationrock avalanche at an elevation above 6200 masl on the western ridge of Mount Chamar in the Sringi Himal. Like a handful of other cascading disasters in the Himalayan region — notably, the 2012 Seti Disaster in Nepal, the 2021 Chamoli Disaster in Uttarakhand, and the recent transboundary Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster — this event was not triggered by precipitation and occurred on a clear weather day. Preliminary estimates based on seismic data and current satellite imagery suggest that the total volume of material mobilized could be between 15-30 million cubic meters, which is nearly one-quarter the size of the initial failure that triggered the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster (estimated at 120 million cubic meters).

Seismic signals from the initial landslide, detected globally in the immediate aftermath of this event, showed that the slope failure began around 4:22 am and suggested a magnitude for the initial failure of 5.1 Mw (Figure 2). With the seismic data in hand, we were able to clearly see the scale of the event, identify the watershed, and see multiple periods of high energy which correlated with parts of the observed pattern of multiple flood waves. (Though, we needed to collect more localized reports to really make sense of this complex multi-episodic pattern.)

On the evening of October 11, a little more than twelve hours after the disaster, post-event satellite imagery (optical, Sentinel-2) from the European Space Agency’s Copernicus program was made publicly available (see Fig 3). This optical imagery provided visual confirmation of the scale of the initial landslide/avalanche and clearly indicated that the flow had come down the steep gorge of a small tributary called the Ungilung Khola, which aligned with local reports. The Oct 11 imagery also suggested that the disaster had originated somewhere above 5,000 meters, in a glaciated catchment, though it remained partially obscured by clouds for several days.

On October 13, our team was invited to the NDRRMA Situation Room to review and help analyze drone footage from October 12 collected by an NDRRMA-led team. This footage, which captured imagery of the Ungilung Khola up to 5200 masl, showed that the landslide had scoured the entire Ungilung drainage but had not significantly damaged the glacial front, apart from the failure of a relatively small part of the glacial snout. This strongly indicated that glacial material involved was not as significant as initially suspected. In other words, this was not a “glacier collapse” as some had previously thought. This relatively small loss of glacial material was subsequently confirmed with other post-event satellite imagery in the days that followed.

Analysis of optical satellite imagery released later that week (as well as field-based visual confirmation, see inset in Fig 5 below) confirmed the location and size of the initial failure. Our interpretation is that when the landslide/avalanche fell onto the glacier, it did entrain some material from the surface of the glacier, including recent snowpack, along with ice and rock deposited on the glacier’s surface by past landslides (exact estimates pending). Remarkably, however, this rock avalanche did not lead to a major detachment from the glacier; so, during this first stage, the flow behaved more like a dry landslide. 

Again, this marks an important difference from the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster, where the bedrock failure triggered a detachment that included roughly 20 million cubic meters of glacier ice. While many are calling this another “rock-ice avalanche” — deploying the same term used to describe the initial cascade in the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster chain (following the bedrock failure trigger that took all that glacier ice along with it) — this initial failure for the Budhi Gandaki seems to have mostly been rock.

After the landslide crossed the glacier, it descended into the steep gorge of the Ungilung Khola where it entrained more rock and sediments along its path. From the source area to the point where this landslide reached the Syar Khola, it fell almost 4000 meters (Figure 3). During the first stage, this flow behaved more like a relatively dry landslide, carrying large volumes of material down the Ungilung drainage and along the Syar Khola to the point where the Syar Khola meets the Budhi Gandaki River. When the flow reached the Syar Khola, it created a massive cloud of dust and an air blast. The extent of this blast can be observed using satellite and drone imagery and by dust deposits in the landscape. Reports indicate that this initial cascade also created a wave in the main Budhi Gandaki River that propagated quickly downstream, although it was to be the smallest of the three major waves to reach these communities.

Downstream, along the Budhi Gandaki River, this disaster was experienced as a series of debris flows. These flows came as pulses or “waves” that propagated at different speeds, though much more slowly than the Bhotekoshi rock-ice avalanche. The first initial flood pulse down the Budhi Gandaki before 5 am was likely faster than the others, given a potentially higher water content (a surge of water forced by the landslide), while the timing and speed of the other flows seem to have varied at different locations along the river course. Most locals who observed the river after the first pulse reported a prolonged period of low flows, where the river ran close to “dry.” River levels continued to fluctuate over the coming hours due to blockages in a variety of locations upstream, caused by a) the initial landslide event, b) debris flows following the breach of landslide dams along the river course, and c) debris flows getting caught in different places along the way, likely causing smaller blockages and surges. Some locals report up to six waves total over a period of several hours, but most report either two or three large waves. The final “third” wave that came down the river after 6 am — almost 90 minutes after the initial slope failure — caused the most devastation.

The debris flow front and highest-volume part of this flow went past the municipal headquarters in Philim between 6:25 and 6:35 AM, according to local testimonies and videos captured with time stamps. As the flow continued downstream, it washed away six houses and a school in Ghattekhola (which was thankfully empty due to leave for the approaching Dashain holiday). This largest debris flow reached Salleri just after 6:30 AM, where it swept away 11 houses and the hydropower project camp, and then hit Jagat just a few minutes later, washing away another 22 houses (Figure 6).

Thankfully, the overall level of loss and damage resulting from this disaster was limited. After watching (shocking and seemingly endless) footage of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster, people in this area were painfully aware of the potential risks of a catastrophic flood. Almost everyone knew to run to high ground when the river started to dry up, and as in Rasuwa, many people also made timely phone calls to contacts downstream, sharing information that helped save lives before government-issued SMS messages arrived. Moreover, people downstream responded rapidly this time after seeing what had happened in the Trishuli River valley. They ran higher than ever before, fearing the unthinkable.

While the jury is still out over the terminology (a common issue with these complex events), one fact remains extremely important here: The lower percentage of ice included meant that the water content of the landslide and the subsequent hyper-concentrated flow were lower. This is likely a major reason why the initial flow didn’t move as fast or propagate as far as it could have. Put differently, if more of the glacier had failed, it could have contributed millions of cubic meters of ice that would have increased the size of the initial flow and could have added additional water (melted ice), enhancing the mobility of the first pulse that came downstream around 4:30 AM NT. Alternatively, more glacial material could have also created larger landslide dams below, adding more water volume to the overall cascading hazard chain or system and  increasing the volume of the debris flows that came later, thus intensifying the system’s impacts. In either case, a higher level of water content could have led to more lives lost.

Reconstructing the Multi-Episodic Debris Flows

During field research conducted in the Budhi Gandaki basin between October 17 and 19, our team collected testimony from a variety of differently positioned local people who had experienced this disaster firsthand at different locations along the river course between Jagat and Lokpa (27 people in total, see Fig 7 below). Information from these interviews helped us to reconstruct the complex interactions that caused and shaped the observed series of debris flows.

Integrating these localized observations with our own field-based observations and prior analysis using remote-sensing data and satellite imagery helped us reconstruct the complex flow propagation patterns that occurred and led our team to the following conclusions:

  1. There were significant blockages of river flow across at least two sites, and multiple landslide dam breach events occurred from these different barrier lakes. One major river-blocking dam was created at the confluence of Ungilung and Syar Khola, and a second was created just downstream of the Syar-Budhi Gandaki confluence, which blocked both rivers (see Fig 7). The most significant breach reported for the upper landslide dam at the Ungilung-Syar confluence occurred just after 5:00 AM NPT (reported by locals in Lokpa), and the most significant breach of the lower dam occurred just before 6:00 AM NPT (reported by locals in Nyak Phedi). Both of these reported events match with the pulses recorded in the seismic data (see Fig 1 above).

  2. Debris from the Ungilung Khola blocked the Syar River several times, both partially and completely, but the river was not fully impounded for very long. Our analysis, based on NDRRMA’s drone imagery and local reports, suggests that some part of this initial avalanche/landslide did get stuck at the Syar Khola confluence, but that this blockage was likely deposited during the middle of the initial landslide/avalanche flow through this chokepoint, after the fast-moving front had come through and continued downstream. Local reports from Lokpa suggest that the river was partially blocked multiple times, with two complete obstructions that led to large debris flows caused by dam breaches: The first flow happened around 4:35 AM NPT (perhaps after a partial blockage during the initial landslide), and then a second and much larger flow was released around 5:05 AM NPT (after a more sustained blockage).

  3. The largest landslide dam was created below the confluence of the Syar and Budhi Gandaki rivers. Material from the initial large landslide from the source up the Ungilung Khola propagated down past the confluence, as evidenced by dust deposits (dry landslide behavior) and local reports. We inferred that a river-blocking landslide dam was formed in this area after the initial event due to the sustained “dry riverbed” conditions reported in several locations below before 5am, which would require a near total blockage of the Budhi Gandaki mainstream, somewhere below the Syar-Budhi Gandaki confluence.

    While conducting field research, locals living above Philim repeatedly mentioned that the Budhi Gandaki River had been blocked, too, forming a lake (using the Nepali term “taal”) in the area around Nyak Phedi. Arriving at the confluence on October 18, our team found clear evidence of this temporary lake, confirming our earlier hypothesis. Our analysis at the site suggests that this dam was formed somewhere near a narrow choke point in the gorge near the suspension bridge that crosses the Budhi Gandaki River just below Nyak Phedi (see Figure 6 below). High water marks indicate that impounded water levels could have been 30-40m above the riverbed (accounting for aggradation) and that water was ponded up to 1.1km upstream along the Budhi Gandaki River. This dam created a highly visible high-water mark, indicating ponded water, which we observed during field research. At present, we are still not sure how long the river was blocked by this dam. It possible that two main blockages and breaches occurred in this area, due to complex interactions with the debris flows down the Syar Khola caused by the failure of the dam near the Ungilung-Syar confluence, but the impounded water level continued to rise around the confluence area until almost 6:00 AM NPT. Full estimates of the impounded water volume here will also require further analysis and flow modeling, accounting for different sequences. However, given the high watermark, we estimate that the Budhi Gandaki River was blocked for a total of between 50 and 80 minutes prior to the point when the lake began to drain following the most significant breach event at 6:00 AM NPT.

  4. The failure of the landslide/debris dam below the confluence of the Syar and Budhi Gandaki occurred just before 6:00 AM NPT, and this event caused the greatest amount of damage downstream. Local observations and seismic analysis suggest that the drainage of this lake occurred over a period of 20-30 minutes. This was likely a partial breach, rather than a single large outburst flood, given local reports from Nyak Phedi recalling the time it took the lake to drain and the river to return to normal and sustained high flows reported/videoed downstream for the same duration.

    The exact causes and mechanics of the dam breach require further investigation. One theory is that a debris flow from above caused an overtopping wave or partial breach. This is supported by an eyewitness from Nyak Phedi (located right above the confluence) who told us that another debris flow full of mixed debris came down the Syar River just before 6 am, after which the lake began to drain rapidly. It is also possible that the flow from this breach encountered and incorporated water stored behind other smaller, partial blockages just downstream (see the next section). In any case, we are confident that the largest and most damaging debris flow experienced downstream was caused by the breach of this landslide dam just below the Syar-Budhi Gandaki confluence at 6:00 AM NPT.

    Critically, local reports of the timing of this breach and downstream flows observed also correspond with the seismic record. The energetic seismic signal created by the rock-ice avalanche and the first wave along the river was followed by a period of quiet until the signal started to increase again at 5:58, which aligns with the time locals from Nyak Phedi reported seeing the lake formed by the nearby landslide dam blocking the Budhi Gandaki begin to drain. The seismic signal then rose again, reaching a peak from 6:36 to 6:43, and then decreased over the following hours (see Figure 1).

Summary of Evidence of a Landslide Dam on the Budhi Gandaki River

Because the finding that a dam formed below the Syar-Budhi Gandaki confluence is one of the most important outcomes of our assessment, we provide a summary of our field-based observations with photographic evidence below.

On October 18, after arriving at Nyak Phedi, our team observed clear evidence of high-water marks at a consistent elevation on all sides of the confluence of the Syar and Budhi Gandaki rivers — seemingly undisturbed by any other debris flows thereafter (see below). Using a phone-based tool, we estimated that this line was roughly 40 meters above the river level right at the confluence, which had reportedly aggraded a few meters. Using a phone-based tool, we took an elevation reading for the high-water mark lines left below the confluence and upstream on both the Syar and the Budhi Gandaki tributaries, and this was consistently measured at ~1680 masl. This extremely stark and obvious line (somewhat like a bathtub ring) suggests a large impounded water body in this area, created by a debris dam.

As we traveled upstream along the Budhi Gandaki River to the northwest of the confluence, away from the Syar River where the main flow came down, we continued to see a consistent high-water mark on the stone and on vegetation. This was a very consistent line at a sustained elevation, different from what would have been created by a sloshing backwater flow (like what occurred upstream on the Kyirong Khola after the initial flow came down the Lhende River to the confluence at Rasuwagadhi during the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster). This line was also inconsistent with what a high-water mark from a previous flood coming down the Budhi Gandaki during the late September cyclone would look like. This line continued up slightly beyond the bridge located almost exactly one kilometer upstream of the confluence at Nyak Phedi, and we found woody debris deposited across this bridge, and then very fine silt deposits just a few hundred meters further upstream, indicating ponding in this area (see Fig 7).

Lingering Uncertainties & Areas of Future Research

Our assessment also highlighted several important questions and sources of uncertainty. What follows is a sketch of two major areas of inquiry where future research is needed.

Linkages to Climate Change: An Open Question

As stated above, this high-elevation slope failure from steep and heavily fractured bedrock occurred on a clear weather day (meaning that precipitation was not a triggering factor). Analysis of this slope using satellite imagery indicates a) that this slope is extremely steep, with an average pitch of ~70 degrees, and b) that several other smaller landslides and avalanches had occurred here in recent years, depositing material onto the glacier below. While snowfall had accumulated at high elevations in recent weeks — causing avalanches in the central Himalaya, including a deadly avalanche on nearby Mount Manaslu — satellite imagery indicates that the majority of snow on the slope had already either slid onto the glacier below (a snow avalanche) or melted by October 11. As with the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster, the absence of a clear weather-related trigger makes formal climate attribution hard.

At the time of writing, no exact triggering dynamics have been identified, and like so many other cases, this likely represents a progressive, complex interplay of geological- and climate-driven processes rather than being attributable to any one factor. Geological structural discontinuities provide pathways along which meltwater generated by climate-driven glacier, snow, and permafrost thaw infiltrates the rock mass. Repeated freeze–thaw cycling and ice segregation then widen these fractures and reduce rock-mass cohesion over time. This, in turn, increases infiltration, creating positive feedback effects between warming, water penetration, weathering, and bedrock deformation. This feedback drives gradual destabilization and progressive movement until the weakened rock mass reaches a critical threshold and fails suddenly. While such longer-term progressive movement has been identified for Chamoli and Bhotekohsi-Trishuli disasters, this kind of analysis is still lacking for the slopes of Mt. Chamar.

It is possible that the southern exposure of the slope which failed could have enhanced more rapid warming of permafrost, and that recent warm temperatures and anomalies in snowmelt could have expedited the pathway towards a critical threshold or tipping point (as established for the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster). But any recent climatic pre-conditioning is entangled with an overall progression of slope instability driven by long-term conditions of thermal and hydrological weakening.

Other Areas of Potential Blockage

This was an extremely complex cascading hazard event, which unfolded over the course of two hours. Field-based investigation and local testimony suggest that each of the three main pulses — the initial landslide-triggered cascade and the two larger debris flows triggered by landslide dam failures that followed — seems to have caused a series of other minor blockages at various chokepoints along the river course. The exact pattern remains uncertain and will require future research. To aid future research, however, we would like to share the following information collected by our team, which hints at one particular area of uncertainty that may be important for future inquiry.

Another important blockage seems to have occurred on the Budhi Gandaki, below a place called Gambul (a single hotel along the path between Eklaibhatti and Nyak Phedi), perhaps closer to Eklaibhatti. While this blockage was downstream of the main dam near the Syar-Budhi Gandaki, the water impounded by this blockage was incorporated into the debris flow that was initiated around 6:00AM when that dam failed, likely adding to the volume of the final major flow pulse.

The couple who operate the hotel at Gambul told us that they observed that the river level had risen and stopped flowing (slack or ponded water) just below their house between 5:00AM and 6:00 AM. While talking with them, they confidently pointed to a place on the opposite cliff about 12-15 meters above the current level of the riverbed where the water may have reached. The riverbed in this area has risen by an estimated 3-4 meters since the disaster due to aggradation, according to locals. The blockage that created this impounded slack water seems to have been caused either by debris deposited by part of the initial landslide or (more likely) by the second wave that came down from the Syar Khola — perhaps the large flow from the dam failure at the Ungilung-Syar confluence reported at 5:05 AM. In any case, the larger flood wave around 6:00 AM appears to have cleared this blockage and incorporated the impounded volume, adding to the volume of that flow but also erasing the previous high-water mark that would have served as evidence of this blockage.

Again, debris flows, especially thick flows like this one, can also get caught or bound up at different chokepoints as they move downstream, creating temporary blockages, full or partial behind them, which may explain differing reports of multiple smaller flood waves observed at various places downstream. To understand these micro-dynamics of rheology, further research and field-based analysis are needed.

The Way Forward: Key Takeaways for Disaster Risk Managers

In recent years, the Stimson Center has conducted several rapid assessments of cascading disasters in Nepal, including the 2024 Thame GLOF and the supraglacial lake flood that hit Rasuwa in 2025, in addition to the recent Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster. But in terms of the intricacy of cascading hazard interactions, the Budhi Gandaki disaster of October 11 may be the most complex we have analyzed to date.

In this piece, we have been at pains to describe the complexity of this disaster because a) the event remains poorly understood, with limited formal analysis published to date, b) we want to demonstrate why an interdisciplinary approach is necessary to decode this event, and c) it deserves attention from national policymakers and the international scientific community.

In closing, we would like to highlight a few key policy recommendations and suggestions about ways to improve post-disaster assessment practices that emerged from our analysis:

Early warning systems must be multimodal, given the Himalayan scale of uncertainties: The Budhi Gandaki Disaster again highlighted major gaps in the existing hazard monitoring and early warning systems in Nepal and the Himalaya region. Like so many other recent disasters, this event started in a place where no one was looking — a blind spot where no one was actively monitoring because no major risks had been previously identified there, either by government authorities or scientists working in the Himalayan region. Since no single monitoring tool or technology will catch all changes and emergent hazards in the Himalayan region, multimodal monitoring systems that use a portfolio of different sensing and monitoring technologies are essential.

Seismic data is extremely valuable for rapid detection: The Budhi Gandaki disaster stands as yet another case study that demonstrates the value of seismic data for rapid detection and basic alerting. In recent years, members of our team have tried to highlight the value of seismic monitoring systems for detecting extreme flow events, publishing papers that demonstrate the potential efficacy of these systems in the wake of the 2021 Chamoli Disaster (Cook et al, 2021) and hosting events that highlight the value of this approach (Stimson, August 2025). Simply put, developing a comprehensive seismic-based early warning system in Nepal that can rapidly detect and locate extreme flow events is crucial, especially when authorities don’t know where the next disaster may occur.

Local observations are critical and contain important data on flow dynamics: While sophisticated remote sensing techniques and sensor data can enable a general understanding, conducting field-based research and discussing the event with local people is often the only way to truly understand a complex event like this. Situated observations by local residents who experienced the disaster firsthand are essential when trying to understand complex hazard interactions or reconstruct the process-chain of such complex cascading events. Information about the timing and duration of flow conditions can often only be gleaned from local observations — by standing together and engaging in dialogue while pointing to specific locations and features along the river (as shown here). Working with photographs and videos recorded by locals are useful, especially when it comes to triangulation, but these often contain only fragments of the context, so conversation is critical to help with interpretation and validation. Investments in training that can help sharpen qualitative methods and data collection practices will pay significant dividends in the wake of disaster.

Locally generated warnings remain invaluable: Strengthening the pathways that can channel local observations and phone calls into an official warning pipeline is also critical. Yet again, this event revealed that local people attuned to changing landscapes and risks are often the first to share alerts with their contacts in downstream communities. In addition, it is vital to strengthen the pathways between phone calls, community reports, and official warning systems, as the residents are the first ones to alert others.  Authorities should continue to develop other advanced technologies for hazard monitoring and change detection but should not forget that timely phone calls are also a highly effective and appropriate technology which complements other alerting modalities. In the face of increasing uncertainty in the mountain environment, it is critical to invest in community-engaged monitoring programs that integrate local knowledge, and investing in these efforts can help create channels for two-way dialogue which are critical when disaster strikes.

Pre-formulating post-disaster assessment protocols and analytical workflows is necessary to improve rapid analysis: Effective coordination between government organizations, scientific experts, and locals is also critical to increase the efficacy and accuracy of rapid post-disaster analyses. Preformulated workflows, combined with routine exercises, can increase the quality and depth of impact assessment, while also enabling the collection of other time-sensitive data crucial for scientific assessment. Rapid post-disaster research needs to go beyond summarizing impacts (headline data on households affected and infrastructural damage) to include the systematic collection of localized information about hazard processes, the timing and duration of impacts, and localized decision-making. Scenario-based trainings focused on qualitative data collection and analysis should be designed for local and central authorities to ensure they are well-equipped to collect and manage localized information when a disaster strikes.

—

Since 2023, the Stimson team and our scientific partners have worked to develop new techniques for multi-hazard risk assessment and repeatedly provided timely technical support and rapid post-disaster analysis to relevant government authorities. Through the iterative testing of different techniques and analytical workflows, we have developed an approach to rapid assessment that we feel is both useful and effective — the analytical process described herein is a prime example. Now, our team wants to leverage our collective experience to help improve the overall system by sharing this approach and training others to use these interdisciplinary techniques, both for post-event analysis and multi-hazard risk assessment.

Going forward, our team at the Stimson Center stands ready to provide continuing support and analysis to Government of Nepal institutions like NDRRMA and the Center for Hydrology & Resources Research (CHWRR) as needed. But, perhaps more importantly, we also stand ready to work with our government partners to co-develop training programs and protocols for post-disaster assessment that will enhance technical capacity and human resources within Nepal.

About the Authors:

Kristen Cook is a geomorphologist and a Research Officer with the French National Research Institute for Sustainable Development (IRD) with the Institute of Earth Sciences (ISTerre) at Université Grenoble Alpes. She is the President of the Division of Geomorphology within the European Geophysical Union (EGU) and an expert in extreme flow events in the broader Himalayan region.

Manish Raj Gouli is a Consultant for the Stimson Center who works as a Multi-Hazard Research Scientist for Stimson’s project on Early Warning Systems for Cascading Disasters in Nepal. In 2026 he has been providing technical support to the Government of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction & Management Authority (NDRRMA), helping assess multi-hazard risks and model complex flows.

Biraj Pokharel is a consultant for the Stimson Center working on a new multi-sited research project on Strengthening Local Disaster Risk Governance in Nepal. He has extensive experience with disaster risk management and humanitarian assistance in Nepal, having previously worked with organizations like MercyCorps and UNDP.

This group of authors has been working together for nearly three months in the aftermath of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster to conduct technical and field-based assessments of disaster impacts and multi-hazard risks. In the wake of the Budhi Gandaki disaster of October, we worked together to conduct this assessment in both Kathmandu and in disaster-impacted regions of Gorkha.

Acknowledgements: The authors of this report would like to thank fellow Stimson team members Dipesh Pokharel, Jeevika Khadka, and Regan Kwan for their initial contributions to rapid analysis, as well as Bikram Karki for assisting with field research in Gorkha. We would also like to recognize our technical colleagues from the NDRRMA who invited us to co-analyze their drone data, including Dr. Prakash Pokharel, Sabin Shrestha, Rijan Gajurel, and Subash Gurung, and drone pilot Shishir Lhamsal. We would also like to thank Dr. Basanta Raj Adhikari for discussing our initial findings in the early days after the disaster, and Dr. Simon Allen for reviewing and providing feedback on this report.

The Stimson Center team’s work on this assessment was made possible with financial support from the Margaret A. Cargill Philanthropies.

President Donald Trump nominated Army Lt. Gen. Patrick Frank to lead U.S. Northern Command and North American Aerospace Defense Command as their next dual-hatted commander, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday.

If confirmed by the Senate, Frank would also be promoted to the grade of four-star general. He’s been U.S. Central Command’s deputy commander since June, serving as the second-highest-ranking officer overseeing America’s military operations across the Middle East and parts of Asia. 

Headquartered at Colorado’s Peterson Space Force Base, Northcom is charged with defending the U.S. homeland from existing and emerging threats. As commander, Frank would also lead NORAD, a binational command between the U.S. and Canadian militaries that is responsible for aerospace warning, aerospace control, and maritime warning for North America.

Frank would enter the role at a time when the commands are hustling to respond to and modernize against advanced cruise missiles, potentially adversarial drone incursions, and hypersonic threats. They’re also shifting away from legacy infrastructure toward software-defined, AI-enabled, and layered defense networks. 

Among other operational priorities, Northcom and NORAD are upgrading systems to enhance domain awareness in the Arctic and supporting Department of Homeland Security-led missions expanding along the U.S.-Mexico border. Northcom was also designated as the Defense Department’s lead synchronizer for domestic counter-drone efforts in November 2024.

Frank would replace Air Force Gen. Gregory Guillot, who assumed the roles of Northcom and NORAD commander in February 2024. Four-star combatant command tours typically run two to three years. Notably, Frank’s career path reflects Guillot’s trajectory — the commander served as Centcom deputy immediately before taking over at Northcom and NORAD. 

Prior to his tenure as Centcom’s second-in-command, Frank served as U.S. Army Central and Third Army commanding general beginning in July 2022. In that role, he deployed for Operation Epic Fury and helped direct air defenses against Iranian missiles and drones following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, according to his official bio. 

Frank also served as Centcom’s chief of staff and commanding general of the Joint Readiness Training Center, as well as in multiple other senior military roles. He previously deployed in several large-scale military surges, including Operation Enduring Freedom, Operation Iraqi Freedom and Operation Desert Storm.

Takeaways from the third Pall Mall Process conference

{"source":"stimson","title":"“Voluntary Is Not Optional”: Release of New Guidelines for the Spyware Industry","link":"https://www.stimson.org/2026/voluntary-is-not-optional-release-of-new-guidelines-for-the-spyware-industry/","pubDate":"Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:32:02 +0000","contentSnippet":"Takeaways from the third Pall Mall Process conference The post “Voluntary Is Not Optional”: Release of New Guidelines for the Spyware Industry appeared first on Stimson Center.","contentEncoded":"

Every November, representatives of governments, international organizations, businesses, and civil society convene in Paris for the annual meeting of the Paris Peace Forum, established in 2018. The timing deliberately overlaps with the Armistice Day holiday in order to highlight the value of diplomacy and multilateralism in preventing future conflicts.

The Forum regularly considers emerging technologies, and in 2026, this was no exception, as 14 governments adopted a set of new voluntary guidelines for the cyber intrusion industry. The Industry Guidelines were developed as part of the ongoing Pall Mall Process, which is a joint French and UK-led multistakeholder initiative to “tackle the proliferation and irresponsible use of commercial cyber intrusion capabilities.” One speaker described the Process as a “wrapper” that brings together fragmented efforts to curb mercenary spyware into a single dedicated forum.

The Industry Guidelines were developed through an iterative negotiated process allowing for input from governments, industry, and civil society stakeholders. The final document acknowledges and affirms the international legal frameworks that underpin it, including international human rights law, the UN Framework for Responsible State Behavior in Cyberspace, and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights. It is organized across four pillars: compliance with regulations and norms, due diligence, risk management, and monitoring of compliance. Within each pillar are several recommended and more specific actions to take, ranging from compliance with export controls to implementing technical controls on access. As noted on its website, the objectives are to disincentivize irresponsible activity and improve transparency for regulators, vendors, and customers while also providing greater clarity for businesses within the industry.

The Guidelines build on and complement a 2024 voluntary Code of Practice for States, which is also organized across four pillars: accountability, precision, oversight, and transparency. The Code is currently endorsed by 27 countries.

Commercially available cyber intrusion capabilities (CCIC) are effectively long-form for spyware, although an important facet of this Process has been its emphasis on the full ecosystem of intrusion tools and services beyond spyware. These same tools are used for legitimate security research and in cyber defense, which has made governance and regulatory efforts complicated.

The Stimson Center has been contributing to the Pall Mall Process since its inception in 2024 through written submissions and participation in diverse global events. Senior Fellow and Cyber Program Director Allison Pytlak attended the November 2026 events in Paris and offers the following takeaways:

  • The threats are real, and no one is immune. Persistent geopolitical tension is fueling demand for intrusion and surveillance tools, while rapid technological development and the spread of AI are lowering the barriers to entry and expanding threat surfaces. Citizen Lab’s new report exploring the first public confirmation of “AdFection” (zero-click spyware delivered via targeted ads), was referenced repeatedly during the conference because it highlights exactly this problem. Similarly, Apple’s new feature, which sends push notifications to users it suspects have been targeted with spyware, has already produced an estimated wave of alerts across 99 countries, reaching targets ranging from legislators and federal government employees in Germany to journalists in Turkey. While a lot of research about surveillance technology has looked at the harmful impact on elements of civil society, no one is immune; the repeated and growing targeting of government officials speaks to the national security threats posed by spyware, in addition to the significant human rights concerns.
  • Civil society cannot carry this work alone. In the words of one speaker, civil society has been the “motor” of the engine driving action on this issue. For many years, organizations like Access Now, Amnesty Tech, and Citizen Lab, among others, have been at the forefront of documenting the harm caused by intrusion capabilities as well as attempting to make sense of one of the murkiest markets in existence. Together, they have assembled a significant evidence base for mobilizing advocacy and action, including as part of the Pall Mall Process. The burden of proof has been met, and what is needed now is the political will and resources for other actors to act on it.
  • Will industry comply? A notable elephant in the conference rooms last week was the low participation from relevant industry actors. Industry participated in the process to draft the Guidelines, but few of the companies whose products and practices are of issue were present in Paris. It has also been observed that tech industry participants in the Pall Mall Process are largely not the companies and vendors of concern. Because the guidelines are voluntary, they will only matter if industry has real incentives to follow them, which makes government action on regulation, procurement, and export controls even more important.
  • Accountability and impact. In a relatively short amount of time, the Pall Mall Process has made great strides in focusing multilateral attention on the problem of spyware and other commercial intrusion tools by developing frameworks like the Code and the Guidelines. Now, these documents need to be put into action. Multiple speakers stressed the importance of accountability in their statements, whether by imposing costs such as through sanctions, by supporting victims, or by adjusting their own activity. In addition, there is not yet a centralized mechanism by which Code-endorsing countries can report national-level action and through which to assess impact. The next phase should focus on helping countries turn their commitments into action, through capacity building and support, paired with a way to track what they do. As stated by the French Foreign Ministry, “A voluntary code is not, however, an optional code: one’s word, given before one’s peers, one’s industries, and one’s citizens, is a commitment.”

events.title: Below Threshold and Under the Radar: How the Annual Defense Bill Could Shield More Arms Sales from Congressional Oversight
events.description:
Previously abandoned proposals to raise the dollar-value threshold of arms sales triggering a congressional review may find new life in closed-door negotiations over a final Defense Authorization Bill, undermining lawmakers’ already hollowed-out oversight of the U.S. arms trade.

As lawmakers negotiate a reconciled FY 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), previously abandoned proposals to raise the monetary value threshold of congressional arms sales notifications may find new life during the closed-door conference process. If included in a final NDAA, proposals would effectively shrink the number of proposed arms sales subject to congressional review and reduce public visibility into U.S. defense trade decisions. With Congress already reeling from years of diminishing authority over U.S. arms sales, the change would represent a severe blow to what remains of U.S. arms trade safeguards.

What Are Arms Sales Notifications?

The Arms Export Control Act (AECA) — which provides the executive branch the delegated authority to engage in and regulate U.S. arms sales — requires that certain arms sales be submitted to Congress for review. Whether a proposed arms sale is subject to congressional review depends on the dollar value of the prospective deal as well as its intended recipient.  For most recipient countries, both the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees must be notified of major defense equipment (MDE) valued at $14 million or more, defense articles and services valued at $50 million or more, and design and construction deals valued at $200 million or more, and are then afforded a 30-day review period before the sale can proceed. For NATO allies, Australia, Israel, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea, the value thresholds are higher and the duration of the review period halved to just 15 days (see Table 1 for details).

Table 1: Review Periods and Notification Thresholds

The notification process is not just a bureaucratic box-checking exercise. It is a lynchpin in a narrow but critically important oversight ecosystem, and one of the only statutorily protected mechanisms expressly designed to facilitate lawmakers’ intervention in the arms transfer process. At the technical level, arms sales notifications trigger expedited AECA protocols that allow Congress to block a proposed sale through a joint resolution of disapproval (JRD). But given the limits of the JRD process — which has never successfully been used to block an arms sale — it is also important to understand how notifications underpin a wider dialogue between Congress, the executive branch, and the American public on arms sales.

By subjecting delicate foreign security partnerships to public scrutiny, notifications have incentivized the executive branch to seek congressional buy-in for potential arms transfers. Historically, this has taken the form of the “tiered review process,” a normative practice whereby the executive branch provides relevant congressional committee leaders with advance notice of proposed arms sales and refrains from formal notification without their approval. Though not required by law, the tiered review process allows legislators to raise concerns, request more information, or suggest adjustments to the terms of a proposed sale. On rare occasions, congressional leaders have placed “holds” on arms transfers of particular concern. Given the structural limits of the JRD process, these holds have represented the only practical tool at Congress’ disposal to effectively block an arms transfer. 

Notifications also represent a de facto transparency instrument. Though direct commercial sales (sales between a private U.S. firm and a foreign recipient) remain obscured from public view, government-to-government sale notifications are posted on the State Department website at the time of their submission to Congress. The practice not only invites public scrutiny but also requires the U.S. government to defend, explain, and bear the political costs of decisions to arm predatory governments accused of human rights abuses or violations of international law. Similarly, as the American public has become more aware of arms sale issues, notifications have proven to be important catalysts for public pressure on elected leaders to take more principled positions against high-risk arms transfer decisions.

What Raising Notification Thresholds Means for Oversight

Raising the dollar value threshold for arms sales notifications would effectively shrink this oversight ecosystem. Higher notification values mean many more arms sales would fall below the threshold for congressional review and under the radar of legislative or public scrutiny.  Information from proposed amendments from the House suggests that the values for most categories would be more than doubled. Senate proposals are less generous but still would raise the notification floors by tens or hundreds of millions of dollars.

Table 2: HFAC and SFRC Threshold Value Increase Proposals

The risks are not simply theoretical. Sub-threshold sales have long represented a practical gap in congressional oversight. Bipartisan congressional efforts to block arms sales to a Saudi-led coalition during its military campaign in Yemen are a striking illustration of this challenge. In 2019, notifications for emergency arms sales to members of Riyadh’s coalition proved a powerful catalyst for congressional action and public advocacy, including the rare passage of several JRDs (though they were vetoed by President Trump). Yet, a 2020 State Inspector General report found thousands of other sub-threshold sales worth over $11 billion to Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in the lead up to those JRDs were spared the same public scrutiny — including sales of the very types of arms that Congress had moved to block. 

In applying the House-proposed thresholds to sales that took place in 2025, it is clear that many proposed sales would have been exempt from notification. Sales of air-to-ground missiles to South Korea, medium tactical vehicles to Lebanon, or medium-lift helicopters to Zambia are just a few examples of transfers that would have avoided congressional consideration. Additionally, higher thresholds could encourage the executive branch to break up larger sales into smaller packages to avoid congressional oversight, especially at a time when lawmakers have proven more eager to reclaim and impose their authority over transfers to divisive recipients.

Conclusion

Proponents of raising notification thresholds have often suggested the reforms would improve the efficiency of the U.S. arms transfer process, noting that the values have not kept pace with inflation. Raising thresholds has consistently featured among recommendations put forward by both executive branch proposals and congressional task forces aimed at speeding up U.S. arms transfers and is a central feature of the Streamlining Foreign Military Sales Act of 2025 introduced by Montana Republican Representative, Ryan Zinke.

But the backlog of U.S. arms transfers that has kept some U.S. partners waiting for years to receive their purchases seems hard to square with the time-bound brevity of the congressional notification and review process. Barring a rare congressional intervention, arms transfers are automatically permitted to proceed after 30 calendar days for most countries and just 15 for NATO+ partners. As for the tiered review process, holds placed on proposed sales are not bureaucratic delays but indications of substantive concerns that merit stronger executive branch consideration.

Long wait times for U.S. defense customers has much more to do with constraints in the defense industrial base than it does with regulation and oversight. Delays experienced by partners are a result of the same systemic production challenges that have plagued the U.S. government’s own struggle to replenish its stockpiles and meet readiness requirements. Within the broader regulatory ecosystem, there may be meaningful ways to improve efficiencies, but by the State Department’s own measures, 95% of foreign military sales are approved within 48 hours. And while the process for submitting notifications may add some administrative burdens, eliminating them would seem to offer a negligible improvement to systemic defense production challenges.

In other words, raising notification thresholds would represent an enormous sacrifice of already-diminished congressional oversight without much upside. And while there may be opportunities to consider where regulations could be streamlined, efficiency should not come at the expense of effective governance and accountability.

From the North Africa, the Mediterranean and the Sahel Program

Events, commentaries and updates from the Stimson Center.

Egypt’s Parallel Inc.: The Myth of Sovereign Efficiency

Stimson North Africa, Mediterranean and the Sahel Program Senior Advisor and Director Emeritus Hafed Al-Ghwell’s analysis challenges the claim that Egypt’s military-run economic empire operates more efficiently than the private sector, and examines its cost to growth and reform.

Defying Gravity: Russian Propaganda in North Africa and the Sahel

In a new policy paper for the Stimson Center’s North Africa, Mediterranean and the Sahel Program, Tom Kent examines how Russian information operations shape narratives in North Africa and the Sahel and why they continue to gain traction despite setbacks on the ground.

Everybody Wants to Rule the Eastern Mediterranean

Stimson North Africa, Mediterranean and the Sahel Program Associate Yusuf Can writes on how rival maritime claims keep Eastern Mediterranean gas in the ground, and what settled seas elsewhere can teach the region.

On Our Radar

The headlines shaping politics, security, and economics across North Africa and the Sahel.

Egypt’s New Administrative Capital Through the Lens of Manuel Alvarez Diestro

Government Deepens Gas Cuts to Fertilizer and Methanol Plants to 33% as LNG Costs Surge

Libya: Dbeibah, Tetteh, and the 4+4 Talks on the Election Path

Egypt’s Private Investment Tops $18 Billion as Government Targets Economic Growth

Suez Canal Revenue Jumps 94% Despite Houthi Red Sea Threats

Egypt’s Foreign Minister Says Country’s Military Is Helping Saudi Arabia Defend Sensitive Sites

Egypt Train Crash in Giza Injures Dozens

AP reports on a train collision in Giza, the latest in a series of deadly rail accidents that expose Egypt’s aging railway infrastructure.

Guinea seeks $19 billion in US and Chinese financing for a major bauxite and alumina project, playing the two powers against each other.
