Tunisia: Authorities Must Urgently Investigate Surge in Detainees’ Deaths in Prisons

India Courts Egypt’s $5.7 Billion Elsewedy Electric for Data Centers and Smart Infrastructure

Indian partners seek to bring Egypt’s Elsewedy Electric into data center and smart grid projects, extending Egyptian industrial reach.

French Journalist Christophe Gleizes Marks 500 Days in Algerian Prison

Gleizes’s family and supporters urge his release as he passes 500 days in detention, a persistent irritant in Franco-Algerian relations.

French Exports to Algeria Fall to €3.8 Billion

French exports to Algeria dropped to €3.8 billion as the diplomatic crisis between Paris and Algiers erodes trade.

French Wheat for Algeria: From 8 Million Tonnes a Year to Almost Zero

Algeria has cut French wheat imports almost entirely, shifting purchases to other suppliers amid the Franco-Algerian crisis.

UN Formalizes Liquidation of Western Sahara Mission

The UN formally began liquidating MINURSO on November 1 after the Security Council failed to renew its mandate.

In Tunisia, in El Amra’s Migrant Camps, a Survival Economy Abandoned to Violence

Report from the informal sub-Saharan migrant camps near El Amra, where migrants stranded by EU-backed controls survive amid violence and neglect.

LNG in Europe: Algeria Replaces Russia and Becomes the Second-Largest Supplier

Algeria overtook Russia as Europe’s second-largest LNG supplier, behind the US, as Europe diversifies away from Russian gas and Hormuz-exposed supply.

AES, Russia, Algeria: What We Know About Mali’s Transitional President’s Talks in Niger and Burkina Faso

United States, China, Russia: Who Are the Main Arms Exporters to Africa?

Islamic State Is Incentivizing ISWAP to Target Military Stockpiles

Egypt: Mada Masr Faces Closure, Editor Risks Jail: Lina Attalah

The Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (HVO) reported that the eruption within Kilauea?s Kaluapele summit caldera, characterized by incandescence, intermittent spatter, lava fountaining, and lava flows from vents along the SW and W margins of Halema`um`u Crater, continued at variable levels during 11-18 November. Incandescence persisted at both the N and SW vents at variable levels during the week. Flames and spatter bursts occasionally occurred at both vents. On 18 November scientists conducted a helicopter overflight and observed high levels of lava in each vent, with a roiling lava pond in the SW vent. The opening of the N vent was about 15 m in diameter and appeared to narrow at a depth of about 15 m, and the opening of the SW vent was elongate, and about 20 m long and 15 m wide. The Volcano Alert Level remained at Advisory (the second lowest level on a four-level scale) and the Aviation Color Code remained at Yellow (the second lowest color on a four-color scale).

Source: US Geological Survey Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (HVO)

The Instituto Nacional de Sismolog�a, Vulcanologia, Meteorologia e Hidrolog�a (INSIVUMEH) reported that eruptive activity at Fuego continued during 11-18 November. Daily explosions recorded by the seismic network, at rates of 1-8 per hour, generated gas-and-ash plumes that rose as high as 1.2 km above the summit and mainly drifted as far as 40 km N, NE, and E; plumes drifted S and SW during 17-28 November. Weather clouds sometimes obscured visual observations. Shock waves and rumbling sounds from explosions were reported almost daily. Explosions also often ejected incandescent material, sometimes as high as 300 m above the summit, and onto the flanks, resulting in incandescent block avalanches that descended the Seca (W), Ceniza (SSW), El Jute (ESE), and Las Lajas (SE) drainages, sometimes reaching vegetated areas. Minor ashfall was reported in El Porvenir (11 km SW), La Candelaria, Alotenango (8 km ENE), Ciudad Vieja (14 km NE), Antigua Guatemala (18 km NE), and surrounding communities during 12-13 November.

Source: Instituto Nacional de Sismologia, Vulcanologia, Meteorologia, e Hidrologia (INSIVUMEH)

The Tonga Geological Services (TGS) reported new eruptive activity at Pelorus Reef, previously referred to as Volcano 8 (cruise designation) or Tofua Arc at 22.8�S (arc location), during 13-16 November. Thermal anomalies were identified in satellite images on 13 and 15 November, rising steam plumes were visible in a 14 November image, and discolored water and floating pumice rafts were identified in images during 14-16 November. Underwater sound signals in the area were interpreted as high-frequency underwater volcanic explosions. The Laboratoire de G�ophysique de Tahiti analyzed satellite observations and acoustic data and reported additional details. A volcanic cloud, 42 km in diameter, was visible at 1300 on 13 November. On 14 November two pumice rafts, 13 km and 21 km long, were located around the emission point. An area of discolored water that was 931 square kilometers was also observed on that same day. Explosive hydroacoustic activity was detected from 1049 on 15 November to 0642 on 18 November by the Laboratoire de G�ophysique de Tahiti seismic network in French Polynesia. A total of 300 hydroacoustic explosions were detected and located at 22.64�S, 175.66�W, near Pelorus Reef. The strongest explosion was recorded at 2036 on 15 on November. Pelorus Reef is described as a large submerged Pleistocene caldera system located about 60 km SSW of Ata Island, 217 km SW of 'Eua Island, and 220 km SW of Tongatapu Island. The W part of the caldera rim was about 35 m below sea level. There are no known Holocene eruptions, prior to the current activity.

Sources: Laboratoire de G�ophysique de Tahiti,Tonga Geological Services, Government of Tonga

Why the Kerch Rail Bridge is harder to destroy for Ukraine 🇺🇦 than the Road Bridge was

The Kerch Road Bridge took at least 10 to 12 drone
events.description:
Why the Kerch Rail Bridge is harder to destroy for Ukraine 🇺🇦 than the Road Bridge was

The Kerch Road Bridge took at least 10 to 12 drone hits before it collapsed. The final two blows were a Palianytsia missile-drone with a +100kg warhead and a Flamingo Cruise Missile with a 1,150kg warhead

Out of those +12 hits only a few did structural damage. The Kerch Rail Bridge arch has much stronger structural support than the Road Bridge did.

The Kerch Rail Bridge was designed for transportation of large freight trains carrying up to 100 metric tonnes of cargo in each railcar, with the locomotive weighing 185 metric tonnes. When combining all railcars and locomotive, one freight train could have weighed at maximum ~7,000 metric tonnes and had over 40 wagons. While the maximum weight of a truck trailer on the Kerch Road Bridge was 40-44 metric tonnes.

The Kerch Railway Bridge Arch is the same length and has 40% less width than the Road Bridge, but the Kerch Railway Arch weighs more.

Weight of each bridges arch:
Railway Arch - 6,000 metric tonnes
Road Arch - 5,500 metric tonnes

The Rail Bridge arch is not impossible to destroy, however it does need to be hit by at least one or two large Flamingo cruise missiles, or repeatedly be hit on the arch in similar locations by missile-drones like Ruta and Palianytsia.

The Kerch Road Bridge was struck by 7 Ruta Block 1 cruise missiles each with a 150kg warhead, at least 4 Palianytsia missile-drones each with a +100kg warhead, and 1 Flamingo cruise missile with a 1,150kg warhead. A total of +2,260kg in explosive warheads hit the Road Bridge, equivalent to around 6 Tomahawk cruise missiles or 11 ATACMS M57 missiles.

Due to the risk of structural damage or collapse, Russia is no longer transporting large Freight trains with significant cargo across the railway bridge, but only transporting the passenger train and going across the arch at very low speeds. CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. 

  • CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. 

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. 

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. 

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Summary

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens products. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

The following versions of Siemens Industrial Automation Software Products are affected:

  • COMOS Walkinside vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • gDAP (gPROMS Digital Application Platform) vers:all/* ()
  • Project Server Web Administration Tool vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC BRAUMAT vers:intdot/>=8.2.0.1|<8.2.0.5 (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC Profiling Tool vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC SISTAR vers:intdot/>=8.2.0.1|<8.2.0.5 (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC Companion vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC OA V3.20 vers:intdot/<3.20.17.1 (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC OA V3.21 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC Unified for Industrial Edge vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC Unified PC Runtime vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC Unified SIQENCE vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC V7/V8 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • TIA Administrator vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • User Management Component (UMC) vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Food and Agriculture, Energy
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-111497
A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream. Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.
Read More

Acknowledgments

  • Siemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA.

General Recommendations

As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity

Additional Resources

For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories

Terms of Use

The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

Advisory Conversion Disclaimer

This ICSA is a verbatim republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-242944 from a direct conversion of the vendor's Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF) advisory. This is republished to CISA's website as a means of increasing visibility and is provided "as-is" for informational purposes only. CISA is not responsible for the editorial or technical accuracy of republished advisories and provides no warranties of any kind regarding any information contained within this advisory. Further, CISA does not endorse any commercial product or service. Please contact Siemens ProductCERT directly for any questions regarding this advisory.

Improper Certificate Validation, Exposure of Sensitive System Information to an Unauthorized Control Sphere, Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key, Missing Authentication for Critical Function, Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Water and Wastewater Systems
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: United States

Vulnerabilities

Expand All +
CVE-2026-117659
The InfoScan Electron desktop client improperly handles TLS certificate errors by accepting certificates without validating their trustworthiness. The client also configures Electron with nodeIntegration enabled, contextIsolation disabled, and webSecurity disabled. These settings weaken the client’s security boundaries. An attacker who is able to intercept or manipulate network communications may be able to present an untrusted certificate without the application rejecting the connection.
Read More

1 Affected Product

Dorsett Controls InfoScan <=1.45.0

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Vendor fix
Dorsett Controls recommends updating affected versions of InfoScan to v1.46 or higher. To install the security patch, user administrators will need to log in to InfoScan and select System Maintenance from the menu. Once the System Maintenance application is open, select Check for Updates, and click the Install Now button in the Ready To Install section. If you are an offline customer (InfoScan has no internet access), you will need to download the update from the Dorsett Controls Customer Portal by selecting the InfoScan Update tile, downloading the update, and following the instructions listed on the portal.

Relevant CWE: CWE-295 Improper Certificate Validation

InfoScan uses hard-coded cryptographic keys and initialization-vector values in its database-encryption implementation. CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-115731 Perforce Puppet Enterprise Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Summary

Background

  • Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

Expand All +
CVE-2026-112136
The affected products MCP Server does not properly restrict its HTTP listener to the loopback interface, leaving it potentially exposed to remote systems. This could allow an attacker with network access to interact with the MCP Server remotely.
Read More

2 Affected Products

Mendix Studio Pro 11 >= V11.15.0 < V11.16.0

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Mitigation
Maintain strict inbound firewall policies (such as Windows Defender Firewall) blocking external traffic on port 7782. This is already the case by default on standard Windows installations. If remote access is required, restrict traffic via a secure, authenticated channel (e.g., a VPN or SSH tunnel) rather than opening direct inbound firewall rules.

Vendor fix
Update to V11.16.0 or later version

Mendix Studio Pro 11.12 >= V11.12.6 < V11.12.7

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Mitigation
Maintain strict inbound firewall policies (such as Windows Defender Firewall) blocking external traffic on port 7782. This is already the case by default on standard Windows installations. Update to V11.12.7 or later version

The affected products MCP Server does not properly validate Content-Type and Origin headers on incoming HTTP requests, leaving it vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF). Utilize modern Chromium- or WebKit-based browsers with Private Network Access protections enabled, or use browser extensions (such as uBlock Origin or NoScript) to block external websites from issuing fetch requests to localhost (127.0.0.1).

This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution.

Actions to take

CISA urges organizations to take the following actions:

  • Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories.
  • Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems.
    • If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access.
  • Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions.
  •  Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes.

Resources

CISA urges network defenders to review the following resource and apply necessary updates:

Vendor Guidance

  • Oracle’s Security Advisory: Critical Security Patch Update – November 2026

Summary

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. events.title: Lessons From the Great War
events.description:
Reflecting on a study trip to France focused on the causes and consequences of World War I. 
The post Lessons From the Great War appeared first on Stimson Center.

{"source":"stimson","title":"Lessons From the Great War","link":"https://www.stimson.org/2026/lessons-from-the-great-war/","pubDate":"Mon, 16 Nov 2026 20:18:46 +0000","contentSnippet":"Reflecting on a study trip to France focused on the causes and consequences of World War I. The post Lessons From the Great War appeared first on Stimson Center.","contentEncoded":"

The Debate on Entering the War

The domestic debate over American entry into World War I was far more serious and sustained than often understood. It is easy in hindsight to treat U.S. entry as the inevitable culmination of a series of German provocations. But that wasn’t the way it was viewed at the time. In reality, the public, the press, and politicians spent nearly three years debating whether U.S. interests warranted intervention, and what a larger military role overseas might mean at home. Visiting crater-pocked terrain in areas of the Western Front and Verdun’s Douaumont Ossuary made clear why many Americans were wary of sending their boys to fight in Europe.  (To be sure, the debate should not be romanticized. After U.S. entry, the government actively sought to shape public opinion and suppress antiwar speech.)

The debate over U.S. entry wasn’t merely between sophisticated internationalists on the one hand and naive isolationists on the other. Many opponents of intervention followed European affairs closely and supported some forms of international engagement. What worried them was the prospect that the United States might adopt the same habits of militarization and armed rivalry that made Europe so unstable.

That concern was especially clear in the preparedness debate. Before the war, the United States maintained a very small standing army by European standards, in part due to long-held fears of large, permanent armies as a threat to liberty. As the conflict dragged on, Theodore Roosevelt and organizations such as the National Security League pushed for a much larger military establishment. Their opponents worried about what would come with it, including higher taxes, greater executive power, and the growth of a European-style military caste that could develop interests of its own.

This debate also raised a broader question that remains relevant. Does greater military capacity merely bolster deterrence and give policymakers more options, or can it instead make intervention easier and thus more likely?

Congress dealt with a related problem as the United States moved closer to war. Even in early 1917, as relations with Germany were deteriorating quickly, lawmakers were still arguing about steps short of intervention, including whether the president should be allowed to arm merchant ships. Opponents warned that the country could slide into war through a series of smaller decisions, without Congress formally deciding that war was necessary.

Compared with many more recent American wars, the debate before World War I looks unusually lengthy and rigorous. Congress has not formally declared war since World War II, and presidents have frequently undertaken military operations without congressional authorization. In other cases, Congress has passed broad authorizations, such as the 2001 AUMF, that successive presidents have stretched to justify operations across the globe.

It’s not hard to wonder whether such a prolonged, serious debate would be possible today. Congress still possesses powerful constitutional tools, including authorization and funding, but over time, it has ceded much of its authority on the use of force to the executive.

Modern military technology has also allowed wars to be launched with much greater speed and secrecy. Presidents can quickly order strikes without first mobilizing a large army, moving hundreds of thousands of troops by sea, or asking much of the public beforehand. This can further narrow the opportunity for debate before military action begins.

What is striking, then, is how long Americans continued to argue over the basic question of whether World War I was their war to fight. Even by the spring of 1917, there was no overwhelming public demand for U.S. entry. Opinion shifted rapidly after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare, but President Woodrow Wilson had not simply been carried into war by popular pressure.

None of this means that U.S. entry was undoubtedly wrong, or that military preparedness was inherently misguided. Germany’s resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare substantially changed the problem facing the United States. But the years before U.S. entry forced policymakers to confront vital questions that are easy to lose sight of once fighting begins.

U.S. Mobilization

On April 6, 1917, the point the United States decided to intervene in World War I, the Army stood at 127,500 and the National Guard around 180,000. Six weeks later, Congress passed the Selective Service Act, federalizing the National Guard and requiring military conscription for all men between the ages of 21 and 30. It was the first draft since the Civil War, and by 1918, the president expanded it to include all men from 18 to 45. A little over 24 million Americans ultimately registered, and 4 million Americans served in the Army in World War I.

The United States instituted the draft because it lacked well-trained troops ready to deploy to the European continent, but also because reliance on volunteers threatened the labor force needed for wartime industrial mobilization. Within a year of entering the war, the Army stopped accepting volunteers to enlist. The Army granted about 100,000 men deferments to support ship construction, whether they had prior shipbuilding experience or not. Still, the deployment of millions of men to Europe created a massive labor shortage that complicated industrial mobilization efforts.

There were thousands of labor strikes in the first six months of U.S. involvement in the war. Metal workers, shipbuilders, coal miners, and others supporting the war effort faced growing costs of living, brutal working hours, and demanding work conditions. Meanwhile, the Great Migration of Black workers seeking a better life in the north and the entry of about two million women into the workforce stoked conflict within the labor force.

One of the worst outbreaks of racial violence in the World War I period occurred when the Aluminum Ore Company hired Black workers as strikebreakers in East St. Louis, Illinois. White workers in an active dispute with the company proceeded to indiscriminately attack the Black population there, murdering between a hundred and two hundred people while ousting about 6,000 people from their homes. The Wilson administration faced sharp public criticism for refusing to intervene. Instead, it focused on war mobilization, primarily through the National War Labor Board (NWLB) and the War Industries Board. The latter operated only from July 1917 to December 1918, with explicit focus on prioritizing war industry needs.

A Decisive Role in Victory But Not in Peace

While the United States contributed far fewer soldiers to the war effort than the other Allies, U.S. entry into World War I did prove decisive. Four years of grinding war had left both the Triple Entente and the Central powers with millions of casualties and desperate publics. The entry of the Americans swung the balance towards the Entente, facilitating their victory in under a year following the arrival of major deployments of American troops in March of 1918.

President Wilson had likewise played a major role in the diplomacy to end the war. Notably, he had sent a peace proposal to Germany in 1916 that was later seen by the Germans as a missed opportunity to end the war prior to U.S. entry. He played a critical role in the Paris Peace accords, pushing his agenda for a League of Nations and the concept of self-determination (at least for the great powers of the day).

But when it came to the final peace agreement at Versailles, the United States failed to positively shape the outcome. Wilson’s failure to secure domestic support led to the first ever instance of the U.S. Senate rejecting a peace treaty. Wilson’s vision of a “peace without victory” was roundly rejected by the Allies, who instead sought maximum concessions from Germany and the other defeated powers.

This would have dire consequences given the animating role of the victor’s peace in the rise of National Socialism in Germany. Our trip to Compiegne, where the armistice was signed, highlighted how the grievances regarding the war’s end became a central narrative for Adolf Hitler. In 1940, Hitler would use the same train car that the World War I armistice had been signed in to humiliate the French as they were forced to sign the armistice for the Battle of France. 

There are books worth of lessons from the end of World War I and the U.S. role, but it was particularly provocative to think about the current role of Congress in ending conflicts and the challenges posed by partners in war termination. Over two consecutive presidential administrations, there has been disagreement within Congress and between Congress and the White House on how to support Ukraine following the 2022 Russian invasion. Like in World War I, while the United States has played a crucial role, Ukraine has given immeasurably more, and understandably feels differently about the terms for peace than the United States does. The United States has struggled to shape the terms of peace because of its own position towards Russia and domestic pushback to any agreement seen as placating the aggressor, both of which have parallels with World War I. The lesson of pushing for a peace without victory is worth remembering as debate continues on how to end the war.

events.title: Everybody Wants to Rule the Eastern Mediterranean
events.description:
How rival maritime claims keep Eastern Mediterranean gas in the ground, and what settled seas elsewhere can teach the region.
The post Everybody Wants to Rule the Eastern Mediterranean appeared first on Stimson Center.

The post Everybody Wants to Rule the Eastern Mediterranean appeared first on Stimson Center.","contentEncoded":"

On October 20, Libya’s eastern-based House of Representatives ratified the maritime memorandum Turkey signed with Tripoli in 2019, and a long contest over the Eastern Mediterranean entered a new phase. Between 2009 and 2015, drillers found large gas fields in the Mediterranean, and boundaries nobody had bothered to draw suddenly mattered. Greece and Cyprus drew theirs on the principle that islands generate full maritime zones. Turkey, which never joined the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, rejected that, and when its neighbors built a gas forum and pipeline plans without it, Ankara answered with the Libya deal, a line across the sea that denies Crete, Rhodes, and Karpathos any seabed rights beyond their territorial waters. Greece and Egypt replied with their own maps in 2020, as Greek and Turkish frigates collided that summer. Since then, it’s been a war of maps.

A Vote in Benghazi

For six years, the speaker of the Benghazi-based parliament, Aguila Saleh, kept the memorandum off the agenda while the eastern camp leaned on Cairo and Athens. Lawmakers removed Saleh on October 6, replaced him with a former chairman of the Libyan-Turkish friendship committee, and two weeks later, unanimously approved it. Quickly, Athens called the memorandum illegal, null and void. Brussels said it infringes the sovereign rights of third states. Cairo called it a clear infringement of Egypt’s exclusive economic zone, and Israel accused Turkey of destabilizing the region. On October 26, Greece’s foreign minister read a joint rejection in New York on behalf of Greece, Cyprus, Egypt, the UAE, Bahrain, and the EU, and Athens and Cairo agreed to open talks on extending their 2020 boundary eastward, into the very waters the Libyan vote assigns to Turkey. Washington called the ratification unhelpful and provocative. But the diplomatic alignment matters more than the words. The ratification has pushed Greece, Cyprus, and Egypt into a tighter bloc and drawn Israel and two Gulf states onto the same side.

Ankara did not back off and welcomed the vote, dismissed the objections, and offered Egypt a bilateral delimitation that, by its own count, would give Cairo more than 15,000 square kilometers of seabed that the 2020 line with Greece does not. Turkey’s case, also called Blue Homeland Doctrine, rests on three claims: that the longest mainland coast in the Eastern Mediterranean cannot be fenced in by small Greek islands lying off its shore, Kastellorizo above all; that a convention Turkey never signed cannot bind it; and that every regional energy structure built over the past decade was designed around Turkey’s exclusion, which left Ankara little reason to respect maps it never helped draw.

Maximalism Is Risky

Each capital can build a coherent argument. Greece and Cyprus rely on the convention text and on the nearly 170 parties behind it. Turkey invokes equity and a long line of court rulings that gave small islands reduced effect against a larger coast. Egypt defends a boundary it negotiated in good faith. Libya wants partners strong enough to back its offshore claims. Both camps have staked out maximalist positions, each has picked the legal principle that favors it, and no principle settles the map on its own.

Yet maximalism comes with a bill. Companies are likely to avoid waters that three governments claim and a fourth patrols. It is unlikely that any international oil company will explore contested blocks while uncontested ones exist elsewhere. Cyprus discovered the Aphrodite field in 2011, and its energy minister now expects a final investment decision in January 2027 and first gas in 2030 or 2031, two decades after discovery. The $6.5 billion EastMed pipeline from Israel and Cyprus to Greece died on the drawing board after Washington withdrew its support in 2022. The Great Sea Interconnector, the €1.9 billion cable linking Greece, Cyprus, and eventually Israel, still has 40% of its seabed surveys outstanding, including the stretch east of Kasos where Turkish warships shadowed a survey vessel in 2024, and its contractor now points to 2031. South of Crete, a Chevron-led consortium signed leases in February for four blocks, and test drilling will not start before 2030. Turkey’s defense ministry called the award a unilateral provocation.

The timing makes maximalism harder to defend. Disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has pushed Europe back into a scramble for gas. The Eastern Mediterranean should be part of the answer, yet its resources sit beneath a map nobody accepts, and the current trajectory points toward two directions. The first is quiet: Blocks stay unexplored, fields stay undeveloped, and the gas earns no government any revenue. The second is loud. A former European defense attaché in Athens rates the risk of a naval incident as very high if any party tries to enforce the Libyan line at sea, as 2020 showed. Every capital has treated the dispute as a contest it can win, and the result is a sea where nobody can drill.

A Shared Map

Functional alternatives may come from outside the Mediterranean. In the Black Sea, Romania and Ukraine spent years arguing over how much weight tiny Serpent Island should carry, the same question that divides Athens and Ankara over Kastellorizo. Romania took the case to the International Court of Justice in 2004, and in 2009, the court ruled unanimously that the island had no effect beyond its territorial sea. Both governments accepted the line. The certainty paid off in 2023. Romania’s OMV Petrom and Romgaz committed some €4 billion to Neptun Deep, the largest gas project in the European Union. In the Barents Sea, Norway and Russia split a 175,000-square-kilometer gray zone roughly in half in 2010 after four decades of talks and wrote rules in advance for any deposit that straddles the new line. In 1979, Malaysia and Thailand set their boundary claims aside, created a joint authority for the overlap area, and have shared its gas revenue since production began in 2005. All three worked because both sides decided that a settled sea was worth more than a war of maps. No Mediterranean government can copy any of these models wholesale, but together, they show that rival states can reach a durable settlement once they find the political will.

A workable Mediterranean deal would borrow from each: direct delimitation talks; a special agreement that sends the hardest island questions to the International Court of Justice or an arbitral tribunal with a scope all parties accept in advance; joint development zones in the overlap areas; and a regional gas forum that admits Turkey. Incident-prevention rules at sea and advance notification of surveys, which Ankara has already floated for the cable, should start yesterday.

Many in the region read the Libyan vote as symbolism, and they are right. Symbols harden into leverage, though, and leverage pays off only at a negotiating table. Every one-sided move, from Turkey’s deal with Libya to Greece’s marine parks and drilling licenses, makes the eventual compromise harder and more expensive for everyone. Shared reasoning costs less today than it will tomorrow, and investors who understand this first will get the better deal.
